n.3: Annual reports are public, not inside information.
n.4: Market gossip is not precise or reliable under CJA definitions.
n.0: Inside information can relate to a wide range of securities, not just government ones.

q: What is the maximum custodial penalty for insider dealing under Section 58 CJA 1993?
w: Section 58 provides for a maximum penalty of seven years’ imprisonment for insider dealing offences.

n.4: Three years is below the statutory maximum penalty.
n.0: Five years is less than the statutory maximum under Section 58.
n.3: Ten years is not the maximum for insider dealing under CJA 1993.
n.2: Life imprisonment is not available under CJA insider dealing provisions.

q: Which of the following is a defence under Section 57 CJA 1993?
o: The insider disclosed the information to friends only
The insider acted on market rumours
The information was already generally available to the public
The individual was not a registered FCA person
w: A key defence is that the information was already generally available to the public at the time of the transaction.

n.4: Registration status with the FCA is irrelevant to the defence.
n.0: Profitability is not a defence under Section 57.
n.1: Disclosure to friends is unlawful, not a defence.
n.2: Market rumours do not constitute a statutory defence.

q: Which of the following best describes 'price-affected securities' under Section 52 CJA 1993?
o: Securities whose price would be significantly influenced by the inside information
Any security traded on a regulated market
w: Price-affected securities are those whose price would likely change significantly if the inside information were made public.

n.1: Not every security on a regulated market is price-affected without relevant information.
n.3: Government bonds are only one type; the scope is wider.
n.2: Director shareholdings alone do not define price-affected securities.
n.4: Foreign exchange is not covered by CJA 1993 Schedule 2.

q: According to Section 56, what must inside information relate to?
w: Inside information must be specific to particular securities or issuers and not general or speculative data.

n.2: General economic conditions are too broad to be inside information.
n.1: Rumours do not qualify as precise inside information.
n.0: Media commentary is public and not inside information.
n.4: Historic data is already public and not inside information.

q: What is a key statutory defence under Section 57 CJA 1993?
o: The person consulted their financial adviser
The person was not directly profitable from the trade
The person was an FCA-authorised insider
The person would have acted in the same way without the inside information
w: It is a defence if the person would have acted in the same way even without the inside information.

n.0: Shareholder approval is not a statutory defence to insider dealing.
n.3: Authorisation status does not create a defence under Section 57.
n.1: Consulting an adviser is not itself a statutory defence.
n.2: Profitability is irrelevant; the offence is dealing with inside information.

q: What is the maximum fine under Section 58 for insider dealing?
w: Section 58 allows for an unlimited fine to be imposed alongside custodial penalties.

n.2: £50,000 is not the statutory maximum fine.
n.4: £100,000 is not a capped figure under Section 58.
n.0: £500,000 does not represent the maximum penalty under the Act.
n.3: There is no set £1 million cap in Section 58.

q: Which type of instruments are included in Schedule 2 CJA 1993?
w: Schedule 2 specifies securities such as shares, bonds, and derivatives including options and futures as covered instruments.

n.4: Property deeds are not securities under Schedule 2.
n.0: Pensions are not included in the list of covered securities.
n.1: Credit agreements are not Schedule 2 securities.
n.3: Insurance policies are not listed in Schedule 2.

q: Who qualifies as a 'secondary insider' under the CJA 1993?
o: Someone who receives inside information indirectly and knows it is inside information
w: A secondary insider is someone who receives inside information indirectly and knows, or ought to know, it is inside information.

n.4: Directors may be insiders but not exclusively secondary insiders.
n.1: Authorisation status is irrelevant to insider classification.
n.3: Retail investors are not insiders unless in possession of inside information.
n.2: Auditors may be insiders if they hold inside information but are not the definition of secondary insiders.

q: Which of the following actions is covered by Section 52 insider dealing?
o: Failing to attend a board meeting
Dealing, encouraging another to deal, or disclosing inside information
w: Section 52 covers dealing, encouraging another to deal, and disclosing inside information unlawfully.

n.1: Board meeting attendance is unrelated to CJA 1993 offences.
n.4: Late accounts are Companies Act breaches, not insider dealing.
n.0: Training requirements are regulatory, not CJA offences.
n.2: Client complaint recording is not an insider dealing matter.

q: What must prosecutors prove for an insider dealing offence under Section 52?
o: That the person disclosed annual results late
That the person was a shareholder
That the person made a profit
That the person was a director
That the person dealt while in possession of inside information
w: Prosecutors must show that the accused dealt in securities while in possession of inside information.

n.2: Profitability is irrelevant; dealing is the offence regardless of gain.
n.3: The offence applies to anyone in possession of inside information, not just directors.
n.0: Late reporting is not part of insider dealing offences.
n.1: Being a shareholder alone does not establish insider dealing.

q: Which statement about Section 58 penalties is correct?
o: They include imprisonment and unlimited fines
They allow imprisonment of up to 15 years
They only apply to companies, not individuals
w: Section 58 provides for custodial penalties up to seven years and unlimited fines for insider dealing offences.

n.4: Penalties apply to individuals, not just companies.
n.1: Fines are unlimited, not capped at £50,000.
n.3: The maximum custodial sentence is seven years, not 15.
n.2: Community service is not a statutory penalty under Section 58.

q: Which best describes the scope of instruments covered by CJA 1993 insider dealing rules?
o: Securities listed in Schedule 2, including shares and derivatives
All pension schemes and insurance policies
w: CJA 1993 insider dealing applies to securities in Schedule 2, such as shares, bonds, and derivatives.

n.3: Consumer banking products like loans are not covered.
n.4: Foreign currencies are not Schedule 2 securities.
n.1: Tangible commodities like gold are not covered instruments.
n.2: Pensions and insurance policies are not Schedule 2 instruments.

q: Which of the following is a general defence under Section 53 CJA 1993?
o: The person gained no profit from the trade
The person disclosed the information to family members only
The person had been trading regularly in the past
The person was not a company director
The person would have acted in the same way without the inside information
w: Section 53 provides a defence if the accused can show they would have acted the same way without the inside information.

n.0: Profit or loss is irrelevant; the offence is dealing with inside information.
n.3: Insider status is not limited to directors, so this is no defence.
n.1: Disclosure to family is not a defence; it may worsen liability.
n.2: Past trading patterns alone are insufficient without showing independent motivation.

q: What must a defendant prove to rely on the 'same decision defence' under Section 53?
o: That they would have carried out the transaction regardless of the inside information
That the information came from public news outlets
That the information was speculative in nature
That the trade resulted in no financial gain
That the FCA had not prohibited the transaction
w: The same decision defence applies if the defendant can show they would have made the trade even without the inside information.

n.3: Financial gain is irrelevant to liability under CJA 1993.
n.2: Speculation is not a statutory defence under Section 53.
n.1: Public information is addressed under Section 57, not Section 53.
n.4: FCA prohibition is not part of the statutory defence.

q: Which factor supports the defence of prior intent under Section 53?
o: The fact that the person held a diversified portfolio
The fact that the person consulted a financial adviser
Evidence that an order to trade was given before receiving inside information
The fact that the person was unaware of market rumours
The fact that the person traded through a nominee account
w: Prior intent is a defence if there is evidence that instructions to trade were given before the inside information was obtained.

n.4: Using a nominee account does not create a statutory defence.
n.1: Consulting an adviser does not provide a defence under Section 53.
n.0: Diversification is good practice but not a legal defence.
n.3: Market rumours are not relevant to the statutory defence.

q: Which of the following is NOT a defence under Section 53?
o: That the decision to trade was made before receiving inside information
That the person already had binding obligations to trade
That the person would have traded anyway without the information
That the trade was required under a prior agreement
That the person gained no profit from the trade
w: Absence of profit is not a statutory defence; liability depends on dealing while in possession of inside information.

n.0: Prior decisions before receipt of inside information can be a defence.
n.2: Trading regardless of the information is a valid statutory defence.
n.1: Pre-existing binding obligations may provide a defence under Section 53.
n.3: Trading under a prior agreement is a recognised statutory defence.

q: How does Section 53 treat trades made under pre-existing contractual obligations?
o: They are always prohibited regardless of circumstances
They are permissible only with shareholder approval
They may be defended if entered before receipt of inside information
They are excused only if FCA authorisation is obtained
They are valid only if executed by an external broker
w: Trades under binding obligations entered into before receipt of inside information can be defended under Section 53.

n.0: Not all trades are prohibited; statutory defences exist.
n.3: FCA authorisation is not required for the defence.
n.1: Shareholder approval is not a statutory requirement under Section 53.
n.4: Execution method does not affect the validity of the defence.

q: Which statutory defence applies if the trade occurred due to a binding legal obligation?
w: Section 53 provides a defence if the trade occurred under a binding legal obligation existing before receipt of inside information.

n.3: Profitability is irrelevant to statutory defences.
n.4: Shareholder votes do not create defences under Section 53.
n.2: Director independence is not a statutory defence under Section 53.
n.0: Using nominee accounts does not amount to a statutory defence.

q: What must a defendant demonstrate to use the defence of 'same decision regardless'?
o: That the securities were widely held in the market
That the FCA was notified beforehand
That the trade was recommended by an analyst
That the decision to trade was not influenced by the inside information
That the transaction produced no net profit
w: The defendant must show that the decision was not influenced by inside information and would have been taken in any case.

n.4: Profitability is irrelevant; intent matters, not outcome.
n.1: Notification to the FCA is not part of the statutory defence.
n.2: Analyst recommendations are not part of Section 53 defences.
n.0: Market size is irrelevant; the test is independence of the decision.

q: Which burden of proof applies to statutory defences under Section 53?
o: The defendant must establish the defence on the balance of probabilities
The burden is automatically on the regulator
The court must assume the defendant’s honesty
The FCA must prove beyond reasonable doubt that no defence exists
The auditor must certify the defence
w: Defendants must prove statutory defences on the balance of probabilities, unlike the prosecution’s burden of proof for offences.

n.3: The regulator need not disprove defences beyond reasonable doubt.
n.2: Courts do not assume honesty; evidence is required.
n.1: The burden for statutory defences rests with the defendant, not regulator.
n.4: Auditors have no role in certifying statutory defences.

q: Which example best illustrates the defence of prior intent?
o: A spontaneous trade after overhearing confidential boardroom news
An automatic dividend reinvestment instruction set before receiving inside information
Selling bonds following an FCA press release
Buying shares after a public results announcement
Trading based on analyst speculation in newspapers
w: Automatic reinvestment instructions set prior to receiving inside information are an example of the prior intent defence.

n.0: Trading after overhearing confidential news is insider dealing, not a defence.
n.4: Analyst speculation is public but not a statutory defence under Section 53.
n.3: Trading after public announcements is not insider dealing, but it is outside Section 53.
n.2: FCA press releases are public; no defence is needed for such trades.

q: Why is Section 53 important in insider dealing prosecutions?
o: It exempts institutional investors from MAR obligations
It prevents the FCA from prosecuting directors
It eliminates all penalties for insider dealing
It provides statutory defences to balance the strict liability of insider dealing offences
It allows regulators to bring civil actions only
w: Section 53 is important as it provides statutory defences, ensuring individuals are not convicted where trades were independent of inside information.

n.2: Section 53 does not eliminate penalties; it only sets defences.
n.4: Criminal prosecutions remain possible; civil only is not correct.
n.1: Directors are not exempt from prosecution.
n.0: Institutional investors remain subject to MAR and CJA provisions.

q: Which special defence under CJA 1993 applies to market makers?
o: They may trade in good faith while performing their legitimate market-making function
They may share inside information with analysts
They may trade using information disclosed to family members
They may delay disclosure until after profit is made
They may avoid reporting obligations to the FCA
w: Schedule 1 provides a defence for market makers who act in good faith while carrying out their legitimate market-making role.

n.2: Disclosing to family is unlawful, not a defence.
n.3: Delaying disclosure for profit does not create a defence.
n.1: Sharing inside information with analysts is improper disclosure.
n.4: Reporting obligations remain regardless of market-making status.

q: What is the purpose of the special defence for market makers?
o: To permit disclosure of confidential information
To exempt them from market abuse laws entirely
To exempt them from all FCA oversight
To allow liquidity provision without fear of prosecution
w: The market-maker defence exists to protect legitimate liquidity provision activities from being classed as insider dealing.

n.2: Market makers remain subject to FCA oversight.
n.0: They cannot lawfully disclose confidential information.
n.4: Record-keeping duties are not removed by this defence.
n.1: The defence is specific, not a blanket exemption.

q: Which special defence under Schedule 1 applies to trading on market information?
o: Where the trade is based on private family knowledge
Where the trade is based on unpublished earnings figures
Where the trade is based on leaked board minutes
Where the trade is made using information that is legitimately available in the market
Where the trade is based solely on rumours
w: Schedule 1 provides a defence when trades are based on information that is legitimately part of the market itself.

n.4: Rumours are not reliable or legitimate market information.
n.2: Leaked minutes are inside information, not market information.
n.0: Private family knowledge is not a statutory defence.
n.1: Unpublished earnings are inside information, not market information.

q: Why is the 'market information' defence important?
o: It excuses trades based on deliberate leaks
It allows trades based on stolen data
It permits insider trades for personal gain
It protects traders acting on legitimate knowledge of supply, demand, or price movements
w: This defence ensures that genuine market activity based on legitimate knowledge of supply, demand, or pricing is not treated as insider dealing.

n.2: Stolen data cannot form part of a defence.
n.0: Deliberate leaks remain unlawful under CJA 1993.
n.3: Personal gain from inside information is always unlawful.
n.1: Directors are not automatically exempt from liability.

q: What is the price stabilisation defence under Schedule 1?
o: A defence for journalists publishing inside information
A defence for shareholders delaying disclosures
A defence for trading based on insider leaks
A defence allowing permitted stabilisation activities after new issues of securities
A defence for market makers withholding disclosures
w: The price stabilisation defence permits stabilisation activity following new issues of securities when carried out under proper rules.

n.2: Trading on leaks is not a permitted stabilisation activity.
n.4: Market makers cannot withhold disclosures under this defence.
n.0: Journalists disclosing inside information is unlawful, not a defence.
n.1: Shareholders delaying disclosure is not part of price stabilisation rules.

q: Why does the law provide a defence for price stabilisation?
o: To allow insiders to profit without oversight
To override market abuse prohibitions entirely
To exempt underwriters from disclosure rules
To permit controlled activity that supports orderly markets during security issues
w: Price stabilisation helps maintain orderly markets during securities issuance and is recognised as a legitimate activity under CJA defences.

n.1: Profit without oversight is never a legitimate defence.
n.3: Underwriters remain subject to disclosure rules.
n.0: FCA enforcement still applies if rules are broken.
n.2: The defence is limited and does not override market abuse law.

q: Which party often relies on the price stabilisation defence?
w: Underwriters conducting stabilisation after a new issue may rely on the statutory defence if rules are followed.

n.0: Retail shareholders do not normally engage in stabilisation activities.
n.3: Journalists are not permitted to rely on stabilisation defences.
n.1: Auditors are not participants in stabilisation trades.
n.2: Regulators oversee activity but do not use stabilisation defences.

q: Which of the following is NOT a recognised special defence under Schedule 1?
o: Trading in good faith as a market maker
Trading for personal enrichment using inside leaks
Price stabilisation following a new issue
Trading to provide liquidity in regulated markets
w: Trading for personal enrichment using inside leaks is never a defence; it constitutes insider dealing.

n.0: Market-making in good faith is a statutory defence.
n.3: Price stabilisation is expressly recognised under Schedule 1.
n.2: Market information trades can form a statutory defence.
n.4: Liquidity provision is part of the market-maker defence.

q: Which statutory document sets out the special defences to insider dealing?
w: Special defences such as market making, market information, and price stabilisation are set out in Schedule 1 of the CJA 1993.

n.2: Schedule 2 lists securities covered, not defences.
n.3: Section 52 defines offences, not special defences.
n.1: FSMA 2000 covers broader regulatory offences, not these defences.
n.0: FCA MAR 1.1.3 sets out civil regimes, not CJA special defences.

q: How must a market maker demonstrate good faith to rely on the defence?
o: By showing trades were conducted as part of their normal market-making role
By obtaining prior FCA consent for every trade
By proving they made no profit from trading
By securing shareholder approval before dealing
By showing they never disclosed any inside information
w: The market maker must show that trades were carried out in good faith and as part of their normal role of providing liquidity.

n.4: Non-disclosure alone is not the statutory test of good faith.
n.2: Profitability is irrelevant; normal trading role is key.
n.1: FCA consent is not required for each trade under the defence.
n.3: Shareholder approval is not a condition of the defence.

q: What does the 'good faith' requirement mean for market makers under Schedule 1?
o: Trades must occur only during market opening hours
Trades must always generate profits for the firm
Trades must be part of their genuine liquidity-providing function
Trades must be approved by all shareholders
Trades must be cleared through the FCA directly
w: Good faith means market makers must trade genuinely to provide liquidity rather than exploit inside information.

n.1: Profitability is not a condition of the defence.
n.3: Shareholder approval is not required for this defence.
n.4: Trades are not cleared through FCA as a condition.
n.0: Trading hours do not determine good faith.

q: Which activity is covered by the 'market information' defence?
o: Using information about supply, demand, or price that is legitimately part of the market
Trading on tips from family members
w: The market information defence protects trades made using legitimate knowledge of supply, demand, or price available within the market system.

n.1: Leaked merger announcements are inside information, not legitimate market information.
n.4: Unpublished earnings are inside information, not a defence.
n.2: Private boardroom knowledge cannot be defended as market information.
n.3: Tips from family members are not a statutory defence.

q: Which instrument issues typically involve price stabilisation activities?
w: Price stabilisation activities are associated with new issues of securities such as shares or bonds to ensure orderly markets.

n.3: Property transactions are not covered by price stabilisation defences.
n.1: Insurance contracts are outside the CJA defences scope.
n.0: Pension schemes are not subject to stabilisation activities.
n.2: Foreign currency swaps are not included in stabilisation defences.

q: Why is the market-maker defence necessary under the CJA?
o: Because market makers must often trade while in possession of confidential order flow
Because market makers should be free from any regulatory scrutiny
Because market makers must always disclose all inside information
Because market makers are exempt from FCA rules
Because market makers act only for their own accounts
w: Market makers may hold confidential order flow and still need to trade; the defence ensures legitimate activity is protected from prosecution.

n.2: Market makers do not disclose inside information; they manage it.
n.1: They remain subject to regulatory scrutiny.
n.4: They also act for clients, not just themselves.
n.3: They are not exempt from FCA regulation.

q: What condition must be satisfied for price stabilisation to be a valid defence?
o: It must be conducted outside market hours
It must always increase the share price
It must be approved by shareholders at a meeting
It must involve directors’ personal shareholdings
It must be conducted in accordance with relevant rules and within permitted periods
w: Price stabilisation is only a defence when carried out under proper rules and within specific permitted time periods.

n.1: There is no requirement that stabilisation always raises prices.
n.2: Shareholder approval is not a statutory condition.
n.0: It must occur during permitted periods, not outside them.
n.3: Directors’ holdings are irrelevant to the defence.

q: What role do underwriters play in the price stabilisation defence?
o: They may profit from insider leaks without liability
They may withhold disclosure of financial results
They may exempt themselves from CJA provisions
They may delegate obligations to retail investors
They may conduct stabilising transactions to support orderly markets in new issues
w: Underwriters may rely on the defence when stabilising transactions are necessary to support orderly markets in new issues.

n.1: Withholding financial results is unlawful, not a defence.
n.0: Profiting from leaks is never protected.
n.2: They cannot exempt themselves from CJA provisions.
n.3: Retail investors have no role in underwriting obligations.

q: Which of the following is a key limitation of the market information defence?
o: It applies only to retail investors
It does not apply if the information is actually inside information
It requires trades to be approved by auditors
It allows trading based on unpublished financial results
It exempts insiders from FCA rules entirely
w: The market information defence does not apply if the information used is inside information rather than legitimate market data.

n.4: It does not exempt insiders from FCA oversight.
n.3: Unpublished results are inside information, not market data.
n.0: It is not limited to retail investors.
n.2: Auditor approval is not a statutory requirement.

q: Which example would qualify under the market information defence?
o: Trading based on confidential board minutes
Trading based on observed order book supply and demand
w: Using legitimate order book data relating to supply and demand is covered under the market information defence.

n.2: Leaked takeover documents are inside information, not market information.
n.4: Unpublished dividend decisions are insider knowledge.
n.1: Confidential minutes are inside information, not market information.
n.0: Unreleased earnings are not market information.

q: What is the purpose of recognising price stabilisation as a statutory defence?
o: To support orderly securities markets during new issues
To protect insiders from liability in all cases
To eliminate FCA oversight of underwriters
To allow firms to profit from leaks
w: Price stabilisation is recognised to ensure new issues of securities are not destabilised by short-term volatility.

n.1: The defence is limited; it does not protect all insiders.
n.2: FCA oversight remains during stabilisation.
n.3: Profiting from leaks is not lawful under any defence.
n.4: Record-keeping duties remain during stabilisation.

q: Which statute contains the specific special defences to insider dealing?
w: Schedule 1 of the CJA 1993 sets out the special defences including market making, market information, and price stabilisation.

n.1: Schedule 2 lists instruments covered, not defences.
n.4: FSMA 2000 contains broader financial provisions, not CJA defences.
n.2: The FCA Handbook PRIN sets out Principles for Businesses, not insider defences.
n.0: The Companies Act 2006 does not contain insider dealing defences.

q: Under UK MAR, what is the effect of Article 15 on market manipulation?
o: It requires proof of intent for any enforcement action to proceed
It applies only to behaviour on regulated markets, not MTFs or OTFs
It defines the four categories of market manipulation
It permits manipulation below a de minimis threshold if promptly disclosed
It prohibits engaging in or attempting to engage in market manipulation
w: Article 15 is the operative prohibition: a person must not engage in, or attempt to engage in, market manipulation. The definitional detail of what constitutes manipulation sits primarily in Article 12, but Article 15 is the rule that outlaws both completed and attempted conduct. The prohibition is technology- and venue-neutral within the scope of UK MAR, reflecting an outcomes-based approach focused on market integrity.

n.2: Article 12, not Article 15, sets out examples and forms of market manipulation. Article 15 contains the ban itself.
n.3: There is no de minimis safe harbour for manipulation under Article 15; conduct within scope is prohibited regardless of size.
n.0: The civil prohibition does not hinge on proving subjective intent where behaviour is of a kind that misleads or is likely to mislead the market.
n.1: UK MAR applies across instruments within scope of trading venues (including MTFs and OTFs) and related instruments, not just regulated markets.

q: Which statement best captures the scope of the Article 15 prohibition?
o: It applies to any person whose conduct falls within the UK MAR scope, including attempts
It applies only where a profit has been realised from the behaviour
It applies only to authorised firms and market makers
It applies only to on-venue trading and never to OTC activity
It applies only to trading in shares admitted to a regulated market
w: Article 15 binds “any person”, covering both natural and legal persons, and captures attempts as well as completed behaviour. The scope of UK MAR then determines which instruments and venues are in play; within that scope, the prohibition is broad and does not depend on the status of the actor or on whether a profit was achieved.

n.4: The prohibition is not limited to shares or to regulated markets; UK MAR reaches a wider set of instruments and venues.
n.2: Article 15 is person-neutral; it is not restricted to authorised firms or specific roles.
n.1: Realising a profit is not an element of the prohibition; the focus is on the nature and effect of the behaviour.
n.3: Off-venue activity can still be within scope where the instrument or related instrument is within UK MAR’s perimeter.

q: Which pairing correctly distinguishes Articles 12 and 15 under UK MAR?
o: Article 12 sets disclosure rules; Article 15 sets stabilisation rules
Article 12 applies to PDMRs; Article 15 applies to investment analysts
Article 12 defines manipulation; Article 15 prohibits manipulation and attempts
Article 12 sets criminal penalties; Article 15 sets civil penalties
Article 12 prohibits manipulation; Article 15 defines manipulation
w: Article 12 contains the taxonomy and examples of behaviours that amount to market manipulation, while Article 15 is the operative ban that outlaws both engaging in and attempting such behaviour. This structure separates the definitional guidance from the prohibition itself.

n.4: The order is reversed: Article 12 defines; Article 15 prohibits.
n.0: Disclosure and stabilisation are addressed elsewhere (e.g., Articles 17 and 5), not by Articles 12 and 15 in this way.
n.3: Articles 12 and 15 are not penalty provisions; sanctions flow from domestic law and regulatory powers implementing UK MAR.
n.1: Article 12 is not limited to PDMRs, and Article 15 is not limited to analysts; both apply broadly within scope.

q: Which of the following is captured by the Article 15 prohibition?
o: Considering a trading strategy without placing or amending any orders
Passive holding of inside information without trading
Attempting to create a false or misleading impression of supply or demand
Publishing a balanced research note with conflicts fully disclosed
Executing a stabilisation transaction under an applicable safe harbour
w: Article 15 extends to attempts to manipulate the market, which includes endeavouring to mislead the market about supply, demand or price. Contemplation alone is not captured, and separate regimes apply to research, stabilisation safe harbours and inside information duties.

n.0: Mere contemplation without externalising behaviour is not in itself an attempt.
n.3: Investment recommendations are regulated under Article 20; balanced, properly disclosed research is not captured by Article 15.
n.4: Lawful stabilisation executed within a safe harbour is a recognised carve-out elsewhere in MAR.
n.1: Simply holding inside information without dealing engages insider dealing considerations, not Article 15’s prohibition on manipulation.

q: Which statement about intent in relation to Article 15 is most accurate?
o: Behaviour likely to mislead the market can fall within the prohibition even without proven intent
Only deliberate benchmark submissions are in scope
Recklessness is the minimum standard; negligence cannot suffice
Subjective intent to mislead is always required to establish a contravention
Intent is irrelevant because only outcomes matter under UK MAR
w: The definitional test for manipulation (Article 12) captures behaviour that is false or misleading or likely to mislead. Article 15 then prohibits that behaviour. The regime is effects-focused, and the absence of proven subjective intent does not automatically take behaviour outside the prohibition where it is of a kind that misleads or is likely to mislead.

n.3: UK MAR is not confined to intentional misconduct; likely-to-mislead behaviour can be sufficient.
n.2: The regulation does not set a universal recklessness threshold for all forms of manipulation.
n.1: Benchmark manipulation is one form among several; the prohibition is broader than benchmark submissions.
n.4: Intent can be relevant evidence, but the analysis also considers the nature and effects of the conduct.

q: Who is within personal scope of the Article 15 prohibition?
o: Any person (natural or legal) whose behaviour falls within UK MAR scope
Only market makers and primary dealers
Only directors and PDMRs of listed issuers
Only individuals employed by authorised firms
Only UK-domiciled persons trading on UK venues
w: Article 15 applies to "any person" and is not limited by employment status, role or domicile. The perimeter question is determined by UK MAR’s instrument and venue scope; within that perimeter, the prohibition is actor-neutral.

n.3: Authorisation status is not a prerequisite; non-authorised actors can fall within scope.
n.1: The prohibition is not limited to specific trading roles such as market makers.
n.2: Directors and PDMRs are not the only persons in scope; all persons are caught by the prohibition.
n.4: UK MAR can capture non-UK persons where the relevant instruments/venues bring the conduct within scope.

q: Which statement about attempts under Article 15 is correct?
o: An attempt is prohibited only if it results in profit
Attempted manipulation is prohibited even if no trade occurs or price changes
An attempt is prohibited only during the primary market auction window
Attempted manipulation is outside UK MAR unless a trade executes
Only benchmark manipulation can be attempted under UK MAR
w: Article 15 expressly captures attempts. The rule targets conduct designed to manipulate, regardless of whether an order executes, a price moves, or any profit is made. This ensures enforcement can address preparatory or abortive behaviours that threaten market integrity.

n.3: Execution is not required; attempts themselves are within the prohibition.
n.4: The concept of attempt is not limited to benchmarks; it applies across manipulation types.
n.2: Timing windows do not confine the prohibition to auctions.
n.0: Profit is not an element; the prohibition is harm-prevention oriented.

q: Which UK authority is primarily responsible for enforcing the Article 15 prohibition?
w: The FCA is the UK’s competent authority for market abuse. It investigates and can impose civil sanctions and prohibitions for contraventions of UK MAR, including the Article 15 prohibition on market manipulation, using domestic enforcement powers.

n.3: The PRA focuses on prudential supervision; it is not the competent authority for market abuse enforcement.
n.1: The Takeover Panel administers the Takeover Code; it does not enforce UK MAR Article 15.
n.0: FOS handles individual customer complaints, not market-abuse enforcement.
n.4: HMRC is responsible for taxation, not UK MAR enforcement.

q: Which statement best reflects how Article 15 interacts with accepted market practices (AMPs)?
o: Behaviour conforming to an AMP can be outside the Article 15 prohibition if the AMP criteria are met
AMPs convert criminal manipulation into merely civil manipulation
AMPs exempt conduct whenever it is profitable
AMPs apply only to benchmark submissions and not to trading activity
There are no circumstances in which behaviour within Article 12(1)(a) escapes Article 15
w: Under Article 13, activity falling under Article 12(1)(a) may be outside the Article 15 prohibition where it conforms to an accepted market practice and the person can establish legitimate reasons for entering the transaction. AMPs are narrow, criteria-based carve-outs overseen by the competent authority.

n.4: Article 13 provides a limited route by which certain behaviours may not be caught by Article 15.
n.3: AMPs are not confined to benchmark submissions; they can relate to trading behaviours meeting strict criteria.
n.2: Profitability is irrelevant to AMP status; conformity with the accepted practice and its criteria is decisive.
n.1: AMPs are not about re-labelling offences; they define narrow circumstances where the prohibition does not apply.

q: Which of the following correctly states the venue/instrument perimeter relevant to Article 15?
o: Only UK-listed equity is within scope; debt and derivatives are excluded
Instruments within UK MAR scope, including those admitted or requested to be admitted to trading on UK venues and related instruments, are within scope
Only spot commodity contracts are within scope
Only derivatives admitted to an OTF are within scope
Only instruments admitted to a regulated market are within scope
w: The Article 15 prohibition applies across the UK MAR perimeter, which covers financial instruments admitted to trading or for which admission has been requested on UK venues (regulated markets, MTFs, OTFs) and certain related instruments, with additional reach to benchmarks and emission-allowance products under the regulation.

n.4: UK MAR is wider than regulated markets and includes MTFs, OTFs and related instruments.
n.3: The scope is not confined to derivatives or a single venue type.
n.0: Debt instruments and derivatives within scope are included; the perimeter is not equity-only.
n.2: Spot commodity contracts are only in scope in specific circumstances; they are not the sole focus.

q: Which UK instrument provides for FCA prohibitions and sanctions where Article 15 is contravened?
o: The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Market Abuse) Regulations 2016
w: Domestic enforcement mechanics sit in UK legislation. The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Market Abuse) Regulations 2016 implement and supplement UK MAR, empowering the FCA, for example, to impose prohibition orders and other sanctions for contraventions including Article 15.

n.3: The Companies Act is not the primary enforcement vehicle for market-abuse prohibitions.
n.0: Money-laundering rules address financial crime controls, not MAR enforcement powers.
n.2: MiFID provisions address conduct of business and organisational requirements, not UK MAR enforcement powers.
n.1: Insolvency legislation is unrelated to market-abuse enforcement.

q: What is the effect of Article 12 of UK MAR?
o: It defines forms of market manipulation
It sets penalties for criminal offences
It establishes disclosure rules for issuers
w: Article 12 defines and illustrates the forms of behaviour that constitute market manipulation.

n.1: Insider dealing is addressed separately in UK MAR and the Criminal Justice Act, not in Article 12.
n.3: Penalties are provided through national law, not defined by Article 12 itself.
n.4: Disclosure requirements are set out in Article 17 and related provisions, not Article 12.
n.2: Client money rules are in the FCA's CASS sourcebook, not UK MAR Article 12.

q: Which activity best illustrates 'manipulating transactions' under Article 12?
o: Entering trades to give a false impression of demand
w: Manipulating transactions involve placing orders or trades that create a false or misleading impression of supply, demand or price.

n.1: Publishing misleading research is dissemination, not manipulating transactions.
n.0: Submitting false benchmark data is benchmark manipulation, not transaction-based manipulation.
n.4: Withholding PDMR trades relates to disclosure obligations under Article 19, not transaction manipulation.
n.3: Unbalanced investment recommendations fall under Article 20 rules, not transaction manipulation.

q: Which behaviour would qualify as a 'manipulating device' under Article 12?
o: Using a fictitious device to secure price movement
w: Manipulating devices are artificial schemes or contrivances designed to mislead the market or distort pricing.

n.1: Selective publication of inside information is insider dealing, not a manipulating device.
n.4: False LIBOR submissions are benchmark manipulation, not a device-based scheme.
n.3: Failure to disclose PDMR transactions is a breach of Article 19, not Article 12 devices.
n.0: Generic research without disclosure breaches Article 20, not the device manipulation provision.

q: What form of manipulation does spreading misleading rumours fall under?
w: Dissemination covers spreading false or misleading information likely to influence prices.

n.0: Manipulating devices involve artificial schemes, not the spreading of rumours.
n.4: Benchmark manipulation involves submissions to a benchmark, not market rumours.
n.1: Manipulating transactions require actual trading activity, not information dissemination.
n.2: Legitimate stabilisation is a recognised safe harbour, not unlawful dissemination.

q: Which action best illustrates benchmark manipulation?
w: Benchmark manipulation arises when false or misleading inputs are submitted to a benchmark-setting process.

n.0: Rumours about a takeover fall under dissemination, not benchmark manipulation.
n.1: Cross-trading to mislead demand is manipulating transactions, not benchmarks.
n.3: Director trade disclosures are Article 19 duties, not benchmark manipulation.
n.4: Unbalanced analyst reports breach Article 20, not benchmark manipulation rules.

q: Which example would be considered legitimate behaviour under Article 9?
o: Conducting buy-backs under a safe harbour
Placing wash trades to move prices
w: Article 9 allows recognised legitimate behaviour such as buy-backs conducted under safe harbour conditions.

n.4: False takeover announcements are dissemination, not legitimate behaviour.
n.0: Incorrect benchmark submissions are benchmark manipulation, not Article 9 safe harbour.
n.3: Withholding PDMR transaction notices breaches Article 19, not legitimate behaviour.
n.2: Wash trades are manipulative transactions, not exempted conduct.

q: What is the purpose of accepted market practices under Article 13?
o: To define circumstances where conduct is not considered manipulation
To exempt firms from capital adequacy rules
To mandate disclosures in investment research
To establish penalties for insider dealing
w: Article 13 defines accepted market practices that allow certain conduct to fall outside the prohibition when conditions are met.

n.3: Penalties for insider dealing are addressed by UK law, not AMPs.
n.4: PDMR reporting timelines are under Article 19, not AMPs.
n.2: Investment research disclosures are Article 20 obligations, not AMPs.
n.1: Capital adequacy rules are under prudential regulation, not Article 13.

q: Which obligation does Article 19 impose on PDMRs?
w: Article 19 requires PDMRs to notify the issuer and competent authority of their own transactions promptly.

n.2: Benchmark submissions are not covered by Article 19, which focuses on PDMR disclosures.
n.0: Investment research is governed by Article 20, not Article 19.
n.1: Buy-back programmes are addressed by stabilisation provisions, not PDMR obligations.
n.4: Client order disclosures are covered under COBS, not Article 19.

q: Who must PDMRs notify of their transactions under Article 19?
o: Both the issuer and the FCA
Both the PRA and HM Treasury
w: PDMRs must notify both the issuer and the FCA of transactions in the issuer's shares or related instruments.

n.4: Auditors are not the recipients of PDMR notifications under Article 19.
n.0: Line managers are not designated recipients under Article 19.
n.2: The legal department is not the competent authority specified under Article 19.
n.3: The PRA and Treasury are not the required authorities for Article 19 notifications.

q: Which requirement applies when providing investment recommendations under Article 20?
w: Article 20 requires those providing investment recommendations to disclose any conflicts of interest clearly.

n.4: Benchmark contributions are covered by Article 12 and 15, not Article 20.
n.3: PDMR dealings are Article 19 duties, not Article 20.
n.2: Safe harbours apply under Article 5, not Article 20 recommendations.
n.1: Reporting stabilisation trades is separate and not an Article 20 obligation.

q: Which conduct is least likely to breach Article 15 when executed strictly within a published safe harbour?
o: Cross trades to engineer closing prices
Price stabilisation meeting all Article 5 conditions
Layering large visible orders then cancelling
Spreading takeover rumours on social media
Submitting false inputs to a benchmark
w: Stabilisation within the Article 5 safe harbour is legitimate behaviour and therefore outside the Article 15 prohibition.

n.0: Engineering closing prices is manipulative transaction behaviour, whereas compliant stabilisation benefits from a safe harbour.
n.2: Layering intends to mislead market depth and is manipulative, whereas compliant stabilisation is expressly permitted.
n.3: Rumour spreading is dissemination and manipulative, while compliant stabilisation is legitimate behaviour.
n.4: False benchmark inputs are benchmark manipulation, unlike permitted stabilisation within safe harbour rules.

q: Under Article 13, how are Accepted Market Practices established?
o: By investment banks through syndicate agreements
By industry trade bodies through voluntary codes
By trading venues through membership rules
By the competent authority following Article 13 criteria
w: Accepted Market Practices must be established by the competent authority against the specific criteria in Article 13.

n.1: Voluntary codes lack legal effect for AMPs, because Article 13 requires competent authority recognition.
n.2: Issuer disclosures cannot create AMPs, since authority recognition is required under Article 13.
n.3: Venue rules cannot substitute for AMPs, because the competent authority must designate practices.
n.0: Syndicate agreements are private arrangements, whereas AMPs require regulatory designation.

q: Which behaviour best describes 'layering' under Article 12?
o: Crossing orders internally to reduce fees
Placing visible orders to mislead then cancelling
Failing to report a director’s trade
Submitting incorrect inputs to a benchmark
w: Layering involves placing orders to create a false impression of depth or demand and then cancelling to move price.

n.3: Optimistic research concerns recommendations, whereas layering concerns order placement behaviour.
n.4: Incorrect benchmark inputs are benchmark manipulation, not layering of orders.
n.2: Director trade reporting is a PDMR duty, while layering is a transactions tactic.
n.0: Internal crossing may be neutral, whereas layering intentionally misleads market depth.

q: Which statement about PDMR obligations in Article 19 is correct?
o: Persons closely associated must also notify transactions
Only shares held directly by PDMRs are reportable
Issuers notify on behalf of PDMRs automatically
Notifications are required only when profits arise
Notifications are required only after year-end
w: Article 19 extends notification duties to persons closely associated with PDMRs as well as the PDMRs themselves.

n.1: Indirect and related instrument dealings can be in scope, whereas the option limits reporting to direct holdings.
n.4: Notifications are due promptly within prescribed deadlines, not only after year-end.
n.2: PDMRs and PCAs bear responsibility to notify, rather than relying on automatic issuer filings.
n.3: Profit is irrelevant, because reporting depends on qualifying transactions not gains.

q: How does Article 12 treat dissemination of misleading information?
o: As acceptable if retracted within 24 hours
As legitimate when sourced from anonymous posts
As acceptable if no trade follows
As market manipulation when likely to influence prices
As acceptable if accompanied by disclaimers
w: Dissemination of false or misleading information that is likely to influence prices constitutes market manipulation.

n.0: Retraction does not cleanse initial misleading impact, whereas Article 12 captures likely influence.
n.4: Disclaimers do not cure misleading content, since Article 12 focuses on likely impact.
n.1: Anonymity is irrelevant to liability, because the test concerns misleading influence.
n.2: A trade is unnecessary, since Article 12 covers likely price influence from misinformation.

q: Which statement best distinguishes manipulating devices from manipulating transactions?
o: Devices use artifices; transactions rely on order or trade activity
Devices require profit; transactions require loss
Devices need issuer consent; transactions need venue consent
Devices are lawful; transactions are always unlawful
Devices require benchmarks; transactions require rumours
w: Manipulating devices involve artifices or contrivances, whereas manipulating transactions involve orders or trades that mislead supply, demand, or price.

n.4: Benchmarks and rumours are separate categories, while devices and transactions are broader concepts.
n.3: Neither category is inherently lawful, because both can breach Article 15.
n.2: Consent does not legitimise manipulation, whereas Article 15 prohibits it.
n.1: Profit or loss is irrelevant, since manipulation focuses on misleading effects.

q: When might an issuer’s liquidity contract be outside Article 15?
o: When performed by a third-country broker
When disclosed only to professional clients
When executed under an accepted market practice
When profits are donated to charity
w: Execution under a competent authority-recognised accepted market practice can place a liquidity contract outside the Article 15 prohibition.

n.0: Jurisdiction of the broker is irrelevant, because AMP status depends on authority recognition.
n.4: Donating profits does not legitimise manipulation, whereas AMPs may.
n.1: Selective disclosure does not create an AMP, since authority recognition is required.
n.3: Timing or venue alone does not confer legitimacy, whereas AMPs do when recognised.

q: Which obligation applies to producers of investment recommendations under Article 20?
o: Submit drafts to the issuer for review
Maintain records supporting the recommendation’s basis
w: Producers must keep adequate records supporting the recommendation and comply with fair presentation and conflict disclosure duties.

n.0: Client identities need not be published, while Article 20 focuses on fair presentation and records.
n.2: Issuer review is not required, because independence is preserved through disclosures and controls.
n.1: Only positive opinions would be biased, whereas Article 20 demands balanced, fair presentation.
n.3: Absolute independence is unrealistic, while Article 20 requires disclosure and management of conflicts.

q: Which off-venue behaviour can still breach Article 15?
o: Internal model back-testing with historical data
Private investment club discussions about macroeconomics
Holding issuer shares for the long term
OTC trades designed to mislead prices on a venue
w: OTC conduct intended to mislead venue pricing may constitute manipulation because UK MAR focuses on effects on in-scope instruments.

n.1: General macro discussions are not manipulative, whereas misleading OTC trades can be.
n.0: Back-testing is internal analysis, while misleading trading behaviour targets market perception.
n.2: Observation alone is not manipulative, whereas deceptive OTC trading is.
n.3: Passive holding is not manipulative, whereas deceptive trading is.

q: Which activity is recognised as legitimate behaviour under Article 9 of UK MAR?
o: Failing to notify a director’s share dealing
Submitting inaccurate interest rate benchmark data
Spreading misleading takeover rumours to increase trading
Carrying out a stabilisation programme in line with conditions
Publishing biased research without conflict disclosure
w: Article 9 recognises stabilisation conducted within specified conditions as legitimate behaviour outside the scope of manipulation.

n.2: Misleading rumours amount to dissemination under Article 12, not legitimate behaviour.
n.1: Inaccurate benchmark submissions are benchmark manipulation, not a safe harbour.
n.0: Failing to notify a PDMR dealing breaches Article 19, not Article 9.
n.4: Biased research without disclosure breaches Article 20, not legitimate behaviour.

q: Why does Article 9 allow stabilisation activities when conditions are met?
o: They guarantee profits for market makers
They exempt issuers from insider dealing rules
They promote orderly markets without misleading investors
They replace the need for disclosure obligations
w: Stabilisation is permitted because it supports orderly markets without misleading investors when carried out under Article 9 conditions.

n.0: Profit is not the rationale, as stabilisation focuses on market order.
n.4: Disclosure obligations remain in place, stabilisation does not remove them.
n.2: Insider dealing rules still apply, stabilisation is a separate safe harbour.
n.1: Capital requirements are unaffected by stabilisation provisions.

q: Which factor must the competent authority consider when approving an Accepted Market Practice under Article 13?
o: The political views of the issuer
w: Article 13 requires the authority to consider whether the practice upholds market integrity before recognition as accepted.

n.0: Profitability targets are irrelevant, while market integrity is central.
n.2: Political views are not relevant criteria for AMPs.
n.4: Shareholder nationality is not considered in approving AMPs.
n.1: Marketing strategies are not a recognised criterion for AMPs.

q: Which of the following is an example of conduct permitted under an Accepted Market Practice?
o: Directors withholding disclosure of share purchases
Submissions of fabricated commodity benchmark data
Liquidity provision arrangements approved by the FCA
Disseminating false information about an issuer
w: Liquidity provision arrangements recognised as AMPs can be lawful even if they influence price, as long as conditions are met.

n.4: False information dissemination breaches Article 12, not permitted under AMPs.
n.2: Fabricated benchmark submissions are benchmark manipulation, not accepted practice.
n.0: Directors must disclose dealings under Article 19, not hide them.
n.1: Recommendations must disclose conflicts under Article 20, not ignore them.

q: How must a market participant demonstrate compliance when relying on an Accepted Market Practice?
o: By obtaining issuer consent before all trades
By filing daily reports to HM Treasury
By ensuring trades always result in profit
By recording shareholder nationalities of all clients
By evidencing that trades were entered for legitimate reasons
w: To rely on an AMP, the participant must show transactions were for legitimate purposes consistent with the approved practice.

n.0: Issuer consent is not a requirement under Article 13, legitimate purpose is.
n.1: HM Treasury filings are not required for AMP reliance.
n.2: Profit is not necessary; legitimacy is the key criterion.
n.3: Shareholder nationality has no bearing on AMP compliance.

q: Which is NOT a criterion for recognising an Accepted Market Practice under Article 13?
o: Degree of impact on market liquidity
Degree of transparency provided to the market
w: Profitability is not a recognition criterion, whereas transparency, liquidity, and confidence are factors under Article 13.

n.2: Potential damage to market confidence is explicitly assessed under Article 13.
n.4: Transparency is a required factor in recognising AMPs.
n.1: Consistency with venue rules is considered when approving AMPs.
n.3: Impact on liquidity is considered when assessing AMPs.

q: Why does Article 13 require Accepted Market Practices to be published?
o: So employees can bypass insider dealing rules
So auditors can confirm benchmark submissions
So issuers can avoid disclosing PDMR transactions
So market participants know the conditions of permitted conduct
So firms can reduce capital requirements
w: Publication ensures transparency, allowing market participants to understand which behaviours are permitted under Article 13.

n.2: PDMR disclosure duties are Article 19 obligations, unrelated to AMP publication.
n.1: Auditors’ review of benchmark submissions is separate from AMP publication.
n.4: Capital requirements are prudential matters, not addressed by Article 13.
n.0: AMPs do not allow circumvention of insider dealing rules.

q: Which of the following is a legitimate reason for transactions under Article 9?
o: Submitting fictitious commodity data to manipulate prices
Concealing director dealings from the regulator
Spreading false rumours about a merger
Issuing investment advice without conflict disclosure
Executing buy-backs in accordance with safe harbour rules
w: Buy-backs executed within the Article 5 safe harbour are recognised by Article 9 as legitimate behaviour.

n.2: False merger rumours are dissemination and manipulative, not legitimate.
n.0: Submitting fictitious data is benchmark manipulation, not legitimate behaviour.
n.1: Concealing director trades breaches Article 19, not Article 9.
n.3: Undisclosed conflicts in advice breach Article 20 obligations, not legitimate behaviour.

q: What is the main distinction between Article 9 legitimate behaviour and Article 13 accepted market practices?
o: Article 9 requires FCA approval; Article 13 requires issuer approval
Article 9 applies only to benchmarks; Article 13 applies only to PDMRs
Article 9 covers specific safe harbours; Article 13 requires authority recognition
Article 9 sets penalties; Article 13 defines insider dealing
Article 9 exempts all trades; Article 13 exempts only dividends
w: Article 9 defines specific safe harbours, while Article 13 requires the competent authority to recognise practices as accepted.

n.3: Neither Article 9 nor 13 sets penalties; they define permitted conduct.
n.0: FCA approval is not needed for Article 9, and issuer approval is irrelevant for Article 13.
n.1: Article 9 is not benchmark-specific, and Article 13 is not about PDMRs.
n.4: Neither article provides blanket exemptions for all trades or dividends.

q: Which is a key reason authorities restrict Accepted Market Practices to narrow circumstances?
o: To avoid undermining the prohibition on manipulation
To remove the need for disclosure of PDMR trades
w: AMPs are narrowly defined to ensure they do not undermine the broad prohibition against market manipulation.

n.4: Profitability is not the reason for restrictions; preserving integrity is.
n.3: Disclosure of PDMR trades is Article 19, unrelated to AMP scope.
n.1: Insider trading is prohibited; AMPs do not encourage it.
n.2: Prudential requirements are separate from manipulation rules.

q: Who must Persons Discharging Managerial Responsibilities notify under Article 19?
o: Both the issuer and the FCA
w: Article 19 requires PDMRs to notify both the issuer and the FCA of their transactions in issuer securities.

n.0: Auditors are not the designated recipients under Article 19; the issuer and FCA are.
n.4: Immediate managers are not notified under Article 19, unlike the issuer and FCA.
n.1: Company legal counsel is not specified in Article 19, unlike the issuer and FCA.
n.2: The PRA is not the competent authority for MAR disclosures; the FCA is.

q: Within what timeframe must PDMRs notify transactions under Article 19?
o: By the end of the quarter
w: Article 19 requires notifications to be made within three business days of the transaction.

n.4: One month exceeds the three-day requirement under Article 19.
n.2: Quarterly reporting would be too late; Article 19 requires three days.
n.1: Annual report timing is far beyond the prescribed three-day deadline.
n.0: Profit realisation is irrelevant; notification is based on transaction timing.

q: Which threshold triggers the requirement for PDMRs to notify their transactions?
w: Article 19 sets a de minimis threshold of €5,000 per calendar year before PDMRs must notify transactions.

n.1: The threshold is not €50,000 per trade; Article 19 specifies €5,000 per year.
n.0: €500 is too low; Article 19 sets the threshold at €5,000 annually.
n.2: Total holdings are not the basis; it is annual transaction value.
n.4: Shareholding percentage is unrelated; the rule is based on transaction value.

q: Which category of persons must also notify under Article 19?
o: Only external auditors of the issuer
Only investment analysts covering the issuer
w: Article 19 extends the notification requirement to persons closely associated with PDMRs.

n.0: Auditors are not covered; Article 19 refers to PDMRs and their closely associated persons.
n.4: Analysts are not obligated under Article 19, unlike PCAs.
n.2: Shareholding thresholds do not trigger Article 19 duties; transaction value does.
n.1: Senior managers are covered only if they are PDMRs or PCAs.

q: Which transactions must PDMRs report under Article 19?
o: Transactions in shares or debt of the issuer and related derivatives
Transactions only in the issuer’s debt securities
w: Article 19 requires reporting of transactions in issuer shares, debt, and related derivatives.

n.2: Global securities transactions are not covered; Article 19 applies to issuer instruments.
n.3: Debt only is too narrow; Article 19 also covers shares and derivatives.
n.1: Competitor securities are irrelevant; Article 19 applies to the issuer’s own instruments.
n.4: Unrelated commodities fall outside Article 19’s scope.

q: Why are PDMR disclosures under Article 19 important?
o: They promote transparency and deter abuse by senior insiders
They exempt issuers from other disclosure obligations
They replace obligations under the Prospectus Regulation
They guarantee issuers’ profitability targets are met
They ensure FCA capital requirements are reduced
w: PDMR disclosures enhance transparency and help deter insider abuse by showing transactions of senior insiders.

n.1: PDMR disclosures do not exempt issuers from other disclosure rules.
n.4: Capital requirements are unrelated to PDMR disclosures.
n.3: Profitability targets are irrelevant; transparency is the objective.
n.2: PDMR disclosures do not replace Prospectus Regulation obligations.

q: What must issuers do upon receiving PDMR transaction notifications?
o: Report it annually in the issuer’s accounts
Send it exclusively to the company registrar
Publicly disclose the information within the prescribed deadline
Record it only in internal board minutes
Forward it to the PRA for prudential review
w: Issuers must publish PDMR transaction information promptly within the deadline to maintain market transparency.

n.4: The PRA is not the authority; issuers must disclose publicly.
n.3: Board minutes alone are insufficient; public disclosure is mandatory.
n.1: Registrar filings are not the primary requirement; public market disclosure is.
n.0: Annual reporting is too late; Article 19 requires prompt publication.

q: How does Article 19 define Persons Discharging Managerial Responsibilities?
o: Individuals with regular access to inside information and power to make management decisions
w: Article 19 defines PDMRs as those with regular access to inside information and decision-making power.

n.0: Not all employees qualify; only those with access and decision power are PDMRs.
n.4: Shareholders are not automatically PDMRs without management roles.
n.2: External consultants are not PDMRs unless they meet Article 19 criteria.
n.3: Auditors are external parties, not PDMRs under Article 19.

q: Which type of derivative transaction must be reported by PDMRs?
o: Currency derivatives unrelated to the issuer
Options or swaps linked to the issuer’s shares
Interest rate swaps not referencing the issuer
Commodities futures with no link to the issuer
w: Derivatives linked to issuer securities fall within Article 19 and must be reported.

n.0: Unrelated currency derivatives are not covered under Article 19.
n.4: Commodities with no issuer link are outside scope.
n.2: Competitor shares are not within Article 19 disclosure duties.
n.3: Generic interest rate swaps unconnected to the issuer are not included.

q: What consequence may follow if a PDMR fails to comply with Article 19?
o: Regulatory sanctions for breach of disclosure obligations
Automatic cancellation of all their shareholdings
Loss of FCA capital requirement exemptions
w: Non-compliance with Article 19 may result in regulatory sanctions for breaching disclosure obligations.

n.2: Shareholdings are not cancelled automatically; sanctions apply instead.
n.3: Non-compliance does not create exemptions from insider dealing liability.
n.4: Capital requirement exemptions are unrelated to Article 19.
n.1: Automatic board removal is not mandated; regulators impose sanctions.

q: What is a primary obligation under Article 20 when publishing investment recommendations?
o: Ensure only positive recommendations are released
Guarantee accuracy of future price movements
Submit drafts to the issuer for approval
Report recommendations directly to HM Treasury
Disclose any material interests or conflicts
w: Article 20 requires disclosure of material interests or conflicts when investment recommendations are issued.

n.1: Future accuracy cannot be guaranteed; Article 20 requires disclosure of conflicts instead.
n.2: Issuer approval is not required; independence and disclosure are essential.
n.0: Recommendations must be fair and balanced, not only positive.
n.3: Article 20 does not require reporting recommendations to HM Treasury.

q: Which requirement ensures investment recommendations are fairly presented under Article 20?
o: Distinguishing clearly between fact and opinion
Reporting directly to the FCA before release
w: Article 20 requires recommendations to clearly separate fact from opinion to ensure fairness.

n.0: Guaranteeing profit is impossible and not required; clarity is required instead.
n.3: Excluding negatives would bias the analysis; fairness requires balance.
n.1: Issuer pre-clearance is not mandated; independence is required.
n.4: Pre-release submission to the FCA is not required; fair presentation is.

q: Why must providers of investment recommendations disclose methodologies used?
o: To comply with capital adequacy requirements
To exempt firms from Article 19 obligations
To allow readers to assess the basis of the recommendation
To reduce the need for statutory audits
w: Article 20 requires methodology disclosure so readers can assess how the recommendation was formed.

n.0: Capital adequacy rules are separate from disclosure of methodologies.
n.4: Profitability targets are irrelevant to Article 20 disclosure duties.
n.1: Article 19 duties are about PDMRs, not recommendations.
n.3: Audit requirements are not replaced by methodology disclosure.

q: Which example breaches Article 20 obligations?
o: Publishing research without disclosing analyst shareholdings in the issuer
Separating facts and opinions clearly in a report
Maintaining records to evidence the recommendation
Disclosing conflicts of interest openly in a note
Using transparent methods to support the conclusion
w: Failure to disclose analyst shareholdings is a breach of Article 20 disclosure obligations.

n.1: Clear separation of fact and opinion is compliant, not a breach.
n.3: Open conflict disclosure meets Article 20 requirements.
n.2: Maintaining records is required, not prohibited.
n.4: Transparency in methods complies with Article 20.

q: Which duty applies to producers of investment recommendations regarding record keeping?
o: Maintain sufficient records to substantiate the recommendation
Retain only oral explanations given to clients
Rely solely on issuer-provided data without notes
Submit all records quarterly to HM Treasury
w: Article 20 requires keeping adequate records to substantiate the recommendation and demonstrate fair presentation.

n.1: Oral explanations are insufficient; written records must be kept.
n.2: Reliance solely on issuer data without notes does not meet Article 20.
n.3: Destruction of records breaches record-keeping obligations.
n.4: Quarterly HM Treasury submissions are not mandated; records must be retained.

q: How does Article 20 ensure transparency in investment recommendations?
o: By restricting recommendations to authorised firms only
By mandating disclosure of conflicts, interests, and methodologies
By mandating disclosure of shareholder identities
By requiring FCA pre-approval of all research notes
w: Transparency is achieved by requiring disclosure of conflicts, interests, and methodologies behind recommendations.

n.4: FCA pre-approval is not mandated; transparency comes from disclosure requirements.
n.0: Article 20 obligations apply to producers of recommendations, not just authorised firms.
n.2: Future performance cannot be guaranteed; Article 20 focuses on disclosure.
n.3: Shareholder identities are not required disclosures under Article 20.

q: Which obligation applies when investment recommendations are disseminated via media?
o: They require issuer pre-clearance before broadcast
They must carry the same disclosures as formal reports
They must guarantee profit if widely distributed
They are exempt from Article 20 duties
They only require disclosure if positive
w: Media-distributed recommendations must meet the same disclosure and fair presentation requirements as formal reports.

n.3: Media recommendations are not exempt; Article 20 applies equally.
n.4: Disclosure is required regardless of whether the view is positive or negative.
n.2: Profit guarantees are impossible; disclosure and fairness are the obligations.
n.0: Issuer pre-clearance is not required for media dissemination.

q: Why are conflict disclosures essential in investment recommendations under Article 20?
o: They remove the need for market disclosures
They guarantee the accuracy of predictions
They help investors assess potential bias in the analysis
They satisfy prudential capital adequacy standards
They exempt analysts from insider dealing liability
w: Conflict disclosures allow investors to understand potential bias and make informed decisions.

n.4: Disclosures do not exempt analysts from insider dealing liability.
n.1: Accuracy cannot be guaranteed; disclosure mitigates bias perception.
n.3: Capital adequacy is unrelated to research disclosure duties.
n.0: Conflict disclosure does not replace other market disclosures.

q: What must be avoided when issuing investment recommendations under Article 20?
o: Separation of fact and opinion in reports
Balanced analysis covering risks and benefits
w: Selective or misleading presentation violates Article 20, which requires fair and balanced analysis.

n.3: Disclosure of methodologies supports transparency and is required.
n.2: Declaration of shareholdings is mandatory for conflict transparency.
n.4: Balanced analysis is the goal of Article 20, not a breach.

w: Risk assessments must consider emerging risks from new products, markets, and delivery channels.

n.1: Tax revenue is unrelated to AML assessments.
n.4: Staff bonuses are not linked to AML risk assessment.
n.0: FCA oversight remains regardless of assessment quality.
n.2: Profits are not standardised by AML processes.

q: Which factor triggers enhanced due diligence for a politically exposed person at onboarding?
o: Earning above the higher-rate tax threshold
Living outside the UK for two years
w: A politically exposed person (PEP) is defined in legislation as someone holding a prominent public function. Because of the heightened risk of corruption and misuse of funds associated with such positions, firms are obliged to apply enhanced due diligence measures when onboarding PEPs. These measures include verifying source of wealth and monitoring ongoing transactions closely.

n.1: High personal income does not in itself create PEP status. The designation is based on role, not earnings.
n.3: Non-UK residency does not automatically trigger enhanced due diligence unless linked to a public function or high-risk jurisdiction.
n.4: Owning multiple properties is not relevant to PEP classification, as the focus is on public functions, not personal assets.
n.2: Using a premium current account has no bearing on PEP status. The trigger is tied to public office, not banking products.

q: Why does the JMLSG guidance require firms to apply enhanced monitoring to PEP accounts?
o: Because PEPs often move countries frequently
Because of increased corruption risk associated with public office
Because PEPs are usually wealthier than other clients
Because PEPs cannot be subject to regular due diligence
Because PEPs are prohibited from holding offshore accounts
w: Enhanced monitoring is required because politically exposed persons hold positions that could be abused for corruption or bribery. Continuous oversight helps identify suspicious transactions early and reduces the risk of financial institutions being used as conduits for illicit funds.

n.2: Although many PEPs are wealthy, this is not the rationale for enhanced monitoring.
n.0: Mobility across borders is not the reason for enhanced due diligence; the focus is on corruption risk.
n.4: PEPs can hold offshore accounts, but this is not why firms must apply enhanced monitoring.
n.3: PEPs are still subject to standard due diligence, but with enhanced measures layered on top.

q: When assessing the risk posed by a PEP, what additional measure is typically required by firms?
o: Requirement to hold assets in sterling only
Verification of source of wealth and funds
Review of personal social media accounts
w: Enhanced due diligence requires firms to establish the legitimacy of the PEP’s source of wealth and funds. This helps identify if money is derived from corrupt practices and ensures the integrity of the financial system.

n.4: Social media activity is not part of mandated checks, although adverse media screening is common.
n.0: PEPs are not automatically refused service; they require additional checks and monitoring.
n.1: Enhanced due diligence does not involve imposing higher fees.
n.2: There is no requirement for PEPs to hold assets only in sterling.

q: Which relationship is most likely to make someone a PEP under JMLSG guidance?
o: Being the spouse of a senior government minister
Being a director of a private UK company
w: Close family members of individuals in prominent public functions are also classified as politically exposed persons. This extension recognises the risk of corruption being facilitated through relatives.

n.4: High-earning professionals are not automatically PEPs without a link to public functions.
n.0: Athletes are not considered PEPs unless they hold public office or are linked to public figures.
n.3: Private company directors are not PEPs unless their role involves public functions.
n.2: Academics are not categorised as PEPs unless they also hold political or state functions.

q: What should firms do if they identify a new client as a PEP?
o: Limit the client’s access to international payments
Apply senior management approval before establishing the relationship
Require the client to submit quarterly income reports
w: JMLSG requires firms to obtain senior management approval before establishing a business relationship with a politically exposed person. This ensures that risks are considered at the highest level of decision-making.

n.2: PEPs are not automatically refused; they require enhanced checks.
n.4: Income reports are not part of standard enhanced due diligence procedures.
n.0: There is no requirement to restrict access to international payments solely due to PEP status.
n.3: Employers are not contacted; firms manage risks internally.

q: Which category of persons is NOT typically considered a PEP under JMLSG?
w: Local government school teachers are not classified as politically exposed persons. The definition is limited to those holding high-level public functions or their associates.

n.2: Senior military officials are typically included within PEP classifications.
n.1: Heads of state-owned enterprises fall within the definition of PEPs due to potential influence.
n.4: Members of parliament are always categorised as PEPs.
n.3: Ambassadors are included because of their political role.

q: Why is ongoing monitoring particularly important for relationships with PEPs?
o: Because they are prohibited from using credit cards
Because they are required to report investments publicly
Because their accounts must be frozen after one year
Because they are exempt from standard due diligence
Because risk can change during their tenure in public office
w: Ongoing monitoring is crucial because the level of risk associated with a PEP can change over time, particularly during or after their time in office. Continuous monitoring helps identify suspicious activities as circumstances evolve.

n.3: PEPs are not exempt from standard due diligence; they are subject to enhanced checks.
n.2: Accounts are not frozen after one year; monitoring is an ongoing process.
n.0: PEPs are not prohibited from credit card use.
n.1: Public reporting of investments is not a requirement for PEP status.

q: When does a person typically stop being treated as a PEP under UK regulations?
o: After they have ceased the prominent role for at least 12 months
Once they relocate outside the UK
Immediately upon leaving their public role
w: UK regulations generally apply PEP treatment for at least 12 months after the individual ceases to hold a prominent public function. This cooling-off period accounts for the residual risk of influence and misuse of power.

n.4: Enhanced due diligence does not end immediately upon leaving office.
n.2: Retirement age is not a relevant factor in PEP classification.
n.3: Relocation outside the UK does not automatically end PEP status.
n.1: Closing overseas accounts has no effect on whether someone remains a PEP.

q: Which of the following best describes an 'associated PEP'?
o: A close business partner of a senior politician
w: Associated PEPs include close business partners of individuals holding prominent public functions. This reflects the risk that influence and corruption can be channelled indirectly.

n.4: Wealth alone does not create PEP status.
n.2: Mid-level civil servants are not usually considered PEPs.
n.0: Private school headteachers are not PEPs under JMLSG definitions.
n.3: Household employees are not classified as PEPs.

q: What type of risk assessment must firms carry out when dealing with PEPs?
o: A standardised checklist of personal preferences
A personality test to assess trustworthiness
A risk-based assessment considering role, country, and connections
w: Enhanced due diligence for PEPs requires a holistic, risk-based assessment considering the individual’s role, jurisdiction, business connections, and potential exposure to corruption.

n.1: Checklists alone are insufficient without a broader risk-based approach.
n.3: Personality testing is not a regulatory requirement.
n.0: Creditworthiness is only one aspect and does not cover corruption risks.
n.2: Geography is important but not the sole consideration in PEP risk assessment.

q: Under JMLSG guidance, when drafting a firm’s high-level AML policy statement, what must senior management explicitly address to satisfy regulatory expectations?
