n.0: Risk disclosures are mandatory and appropriate.
n.2: Plain language supports clarity and is encouraged.
n.3: Benchmarks provide useful context when applied correctly.
n.1: Advising clients that tax treatment may change is required.

q: Which element must be included when disclosing costs and charges in a financial promotion?
o: A vague reference to possible fees
A disclaimer that costs are uncertain
All costs and charges in aggregated and itemised form
w: The FCA requires disclosure of all costs and charges, presented clearly and in detail, so clients can understand the full impact on their investment.

n.3: Initial charges alone would understate total costs.
n.0: Vague references fail to give the necessary transparency.
n.2: Costs are not limited to performance-based fees.
n.1: Costs must be explained, not dismissed as uncertain.

q: According to COBS, what is the main purpose of requiring financial promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading?
o: To ensure firms maximise sales of financial products
To comply only with advertising industry codes
To protect clients by allowing informed decisions
To reduce the length of promotional documents
w: The purpose of this rule is to protect clients, particularly retail clients, by ensuring they receive information that enables them to make informed and balanced decisions about financial products or services.

n.0: Maximising sales is not the regulatory objective; client protection is.
n.2: The requirement is FCA-driven, not based only on advertising codes.
n.1: While competition may result, the rule’s aim is consumer protection.
n.4: Length reduction is not relevant; clarity and fairness are.

q: Under COBS, when is it acceptable to omit material information in client communications?
o: When it would confuse the client
When the FCA gives verbal consent
When the omission makes the promotion more appealing
When the firm believes the client already knows the risks
When it is not relevant to the product or service offered
w: Material information can only be omitted if it is genuinely irrelevant to the product or service being described. Otherwise, omission would mislead the client and breach FCA rules.

n.0: Information should be explained clearly rather than omitted.
n.3: Firms cannot assume knowledge; all relevant information must be provided.
n.2: Omissions that improve appeal would mislead clients and breach the rule.
n.1: The FCA does not permit omissions based on verbal consent.

q: When firms use comparisons in financial promotions, what must they ensure?
o: That the comparison is fair, meaningful and presented in a balanced way
That comparisons are based on future projections only
That only positive features of their product are compared
w: Any comparisons must be accurate, fair and balanced, enabling the client to make a meaningful evaluation without being misled.

n.4: Highlighting only positives is misleading and not permitted.
n.3: Comparisons must be based on objective, verifiable data, not solely projections.
n.1: Benchmarks may be useful when applied appropriately.
n.0: Competitors can be named if done fairly and objectively.

q: Which disclosure is mandatory when including simulated past performance in client communications?
o: That simulated performance is equivalent to actual performance
That the FCA has endorsed the figures
That risks are not applicable to hypothetical data
That the figures are hypothetical and based on assumptions
w: Simulated past performance must be clearly identified as hypothetical, with explanation of the assumptions used, so clients do not confuse it with real results.

n.0: Equating simulated and actual performance would mislead clients.
n.3: Guarantees cannot be made on hypothetical data.
n.1: The FCA does not endorse figures within promotions.
n.2: Risks still apply; assumptions may not hold true.

q: Under COBS rules, what must a firm ensure about risk warnings in financial promotions?
o: They are prominent and in the same language as the promotion
They are in small print at the end of the document
They may be replaced with generic disclaimers
They can be omitted if the client is sophisticated
They must only be provided verbally
w: Risk warnings must be clear, prominent, and in the same language as the promotion to ensure clients properly understand the risks involved.

n.1: Small print warnings do not meet prominence requirements.
n.3: Sophisticated clients are still entitled to clear disclosures.
n.2: Generic disclaimers are insufficient; risks must be specific and clear.
n.4: Risk warnings must appear in the written material itself.

q: What additional disclosure is required when presenting gross performance figures in a financial promotion?
o: That tax is irrelevant to performance outcomes
That gross performance is superior to net performance
That all charges and commissions will reduce the actual return
That clients will definitely achieve higher returns
w: Where gross performance is shown, firms must disclose that charges, commissions and fees will reduce actual returns, ensuring clients are not misled about outcomes.

n.3: The FCA does not guarantee returns.
n.4: Promotions must not imply certainty of higher returns.
n.1: Stating superiority would be misleading; both must be shown transparently.
n.0: Tax must be considered; it can affect actual performance.

q: In relation to COBS 4.5, what applies when firms communicate with retail clients about MiFID products?
o: Communications must be fair, clear, not misleading and show risks and benefits equally
Charges can be excluded if they are complex
Firms can downplay risks if they provide advice
Benefits may be highlighted over risks
MiFID retail clients are exempt from financial promotions standards
w: COBS 4.5 requires that MiFID retail promotions be balanced, presenting risks and benefits with equal prominence to safeguard clients from bias.

n.2: Risks cannot be downplayed even with advice.
n.3: Highlighting benefits disproportionately would breach rules.
n.4: MiFID retail clients are subject to stricter, not looser, standards.
n.1: Charges must be disclosed, regardless of complexity.

q: Which of the following statements about financial promotions is TRUE under FCA rules?
o: They are only regulated if issued in print form
They can imply FCA endorsement if authorised
They can ignore likely audience sophistication
They must be accurate and not create false impressions
They must always be drafted in technical legal language
w: Promotions must be accurate, balanced and not misleading in any format, including online, to ensure clients are not given false impressions.

n.4: Technical legal language is not required; clarity is.
n.2: Communications must match the sophistication of the target audience.
n.0: The rules apply across all media, not just print.
n.1: Implying FCA endorsement is prohibited.

q: When using forecasts in a financial promotion, what is required?
o: Forecasts may be exaggerated to attract interest
Forecasts can be shown without risk warnings
Forecasts are prohibited in all circumstances
Forecasts must imply guaranteed future outcomes
Forecasts must be based on reasonable assumptions and clearly disclosed as estimates
w: Forecasts may be used if based on reasonable assumptions and accompanied by prominent disclosure that they are estimates and subject to risks.

n.0: Exaggeration would mislead and breach FCA rules.
n.1: Risk warnings must always accompany forecasts.
n.3: Outcomes can never be guaranteed in forecasts.
n.2: Forecasts are permitted if used responsibly with required disclosures.

q: Which of the following must be avoided in financial promotions under FCA rules?
o: Stating that tax rules may change in future
Clear disclosure of fees and charges
Use of benchmarks for meaningful comparison
Balanced presentation of risks and rewards
Use of misleading titles or names that disguise risk
w: Misleading titles, names or labels that disguise the true risk or nature of the product must be avoided, as they breach the requirement for fair, clear and not misleading communication.

n.3: Balanced presentation is required, not prohibited.
n.1: Fees and charges must be disclosed clearly.
n.2: Benchmarks are allowed if they support fair comparison.
n.0: Tax variability must be highlighted, not avoided.

q: Which of the following is REQUIRED when a promotion includes comparisons of past performance?
o: Figures must cover at least the previous five years if available
Past performance can be implied to guarantee future outcomes
Only the best-performing years may be selected
Figures may be shown without reference to benchmarks
Comparisons can be limited to two favourable months
w: Where past performance is shown, it must cover at least five years if available, presented in a balanced manner with clear warnings that it is not a guide to the future.

n.2: Cherry-picking good years would mislead clients.
n.4: Selecting short favourable periods breaches balance requirements.
n.1: Past performance must never be presented as a guarantee.
n.3: Benchmarks should be included for meaningful context.

q: Under FCA rules, what is the primary requirement for communications to retail clients regarding charges?
o: Charges can be omitted if they are complex
Charges disclosure is optional if advice is provided
Charges must be disclosed in a clear, itemised and aggregate form
Charges may be described vaguely as ‘industry standard’
w: Charges must be transparent, shown in both aggregated and itemised form, to ensure retail clients fully understand the costs of products and services.

n.0: All charges, not just initial ones, must be disclosed.
n.4: Vague terms do not provide transparency.
n.1: Complexity does not excuse non-disclosure.
n.2: Advice does not remove the duty of disclosure.

q: What must a firm ensure if a financial promotion is targeted at a specific audience segment?
o: That it implies FCA endorsement of the content
That it focuses solely on product advantages
That it uses complex terminology to impress clients
That the communication is appropriate for the likely knowledge of that audience
That it excludes risk information for simplicity
w: Firms must tailor promotions so they are clear, fair and not misleading to the likely audience, taking account of their knowledge and experience.

n.2: Complex language undermines clarity and can mislead.
n.4: Risk information must always be disclosed clearly.
n.1: Advantages alone without risks would create bias.
n.0: FCA endorsement cannot be implied.

q: Which requirement applies when quoting gross yield figures in promotions?
o: They can be presented as guaranteed outcomes
They must be accompanied by a disclosure that charges reduce actual returns
They can be shown without explanation if they are positive
They must be higher than net yields
w: Gross yield figures must be accompanied by a clear explanation that fees, charges and tax will reduce actual returns, ensuring transparency.

n.3: Figures must always be explained, not left ambiguous.
n.4: No requirement exists that gross must be higher; both must be presented accurately.
n.0: Tax implications must not be omitted.
n.1: Outcomes cannot be guaranteed.

q: In Non-MiFID promotions under COBS 4.2, how must firms treat information on risks?
o: Provide risks with equal prominence to benefits
Disclose risks separately in a different document
Omit risks if the product is simple
Only disclose risks if requested by the client
w: COBS 4.2 requires that risk disclosures be clear, specific and given the same prominence as benefits, preventing biased or misleading impressions.

n.4: Risks must always be disclosed, not just when requested.
n.3: Even simple products require risk disclosures.
n.2: Risks must appear within the same communication, not elsewhere.
n.0: Generic disclaimers are insufficient; specific risks must be stated.

q: Which of the following is a requirement under COBS for the presentation of investment returns?
o: Returns can be based on selective time periods only
Returns must not be presented as guaranteed unless they are genuinely risk-free
Firms may emphasise best-case scenarios only
Returns may be quoted without disclosing fees
Returns can be presented in isolation from risk information
w: COBS rules prevent returns being described as guaranteed unless they are genuinely risk-free. All claims must be fair, balanced and supported by risk disclosures.

n.2: Best-case only is misleading; balanced outcomes must be shown.
n.3: Fees must always be disclosed to show the true net return.
n.4: Returns cannot be presented without risk information.
n.0: Selective periods distort the picture and are not allowed.

q: Under FCA COBS rules, when is it acceptable to present forecasts in absolute monetary terms?
o: When no basis for the calculation is provided
When the firm wants to emphasise growth potential
When they are based on reasonable assumptions and include risk disclosures
When authorised by the FCA on a case-by-case basis
w: Forecasts may be shown in monetary terms if they are based on reasonable assumptions, explained clearly, and accompanied by disclosures about risks and uncertainties.

n.2: Emphasising growth without explanation would mislead.
n.1: Forecasts must always have a clear basis.
n.0: Tax treatment must be explained, not excluded.
n.4: FCA does not approve forecasts individually; firms are responsible for compliance.

q: Which principle underpins all financial promotions to retail clients under both MiFID and Non-MiFID COBS?
o: They must be drafted in legal language
They must be fair, clear and not misleading
w: The overarching principle is that all communications and promotions must be fair, clear and not misleading, regardless of product type or business classification.

n.1: The purpose is client protection, not sales maximisation.
n.2: Tax advantages cannot be guaranteed.
n.4: Performance information can be included if presented correctly.
n.0: Clarity is required; legal jargon may undermine this.

q: Which of the following is a breach of FCA requirements for retail promotions?
o: Use of exaggerated claims about potential returns
Disclosure of charges in clear terms
Use of plain language to explain features
Inclusion of warnings about tax changes
Balanced presentation of risks and benefits
w: Exaggerated claims about returns create misleading impressions and are prohibited under the 'fair, clear and not misleading' standard.

n.4: Balanced presentation is compliant and required.
n.1: Clear disclosure of charges is required, not a breach.
n.3: Warning clients of tax changes is correct practice.
n.2: Plain language supports clarity and is encouraged.

q: What does ‘fair’ mean in the context of FCA client communications?
o: That the firm only provides the most positive scenarios
That the firm can omit charges if small
That the firm prioritises sales over accuracy
That the communication gives a balanced view of benefits and risks
That the communication favours the most profitable clients
w: Fairness means presenting a balanced view of the product or service, showing both risks and rewards, enabling clients to make properly informed decisions.

n.2: Prioritising sales over accuracy would breach fairness.
n.4: Favouring certain clients is not relevant to fairness.
n.1: Charges must be disclosed regardless of size.
n.0: Only positive scenarios would not be fair or balanced.

q: Which of the following statements about financial promotions under FCA rules is TRUE?
o: They only need to be clear if aimed at professional clients
They can guarantee returns to retail clients
They may exclude charges if these are difficult to calculate
They must avoid implying that products are risk-free unless they genuinely are
They may rely on disclaimers alone to offset misleading impressions
w: Promotions must never suggest that products are risk-free unless that is factually correct, and all risks must be disclosed clearly.

n.1: Returns cannot be guaranteed; outcomes must always include risk disclosure.
n.2: Charges must be disclosed, regardless of complexity.
n.4: Disclaimers alone cannot correct a misleading impression.
n.0: Clarity applies to all clients, not just professionals.

q: What is required when financial promotions include statements about future tax treatment?
o: That tax treatment is irrelevant to investment outcomes
A warning that tax treatment depends on individual circumstances and may change
That all clients will benefit equally from tax reliefs
An assurance that the tax position will remain constant
w: Promotions must state that tax treatment depends on the investor’s personal circumstances and is subject to change, ensuring clients are not misled.

n.3: No assurance can be given that tax rules will remain unchanged.
n.2: Not all clients benefit equally from tax reliefs.
n.4: The FCA does not guarantee tax advantages.
n.0: Tax treatment can significantly affect outcomes.

q: What does 'not misleading' mean in the context of FCA communications?
o: That only professional clients are protected
That disclaimers are sufficient to protect against liability
That firms can emphasise positives without mentioning risks
That figures can be exaggerated if explained in small print
That communications must not create false or distorted impressions
w: Not misleading means the communication must not give a false or distorted impression, whether by omission, exaggeration or selective presentation.

n.2: Risks must be disclosed alongside benefits.
n.1: Disclaimers cannot correct an overall misleading impression.
n.3: Exaggerated figures breach fairness and accuracy.
n.0: The rule protects all client categories, not just professionals.

q: Which of the following would breach COBS rules on financial promotions?
o: Cherry-picking favourable time periods for performance data
Using plain language to explain products
Warning that tax rules may change
Providing equal prominence to risks and benefits
w: Selecting only favourable time periods for performance data misleads clients and breaches the fair, clear and not misleading requirement.

n.4: Equal prominence is required, not a breach.
n.1: Clear charge disclosure is compliant with FCA rules.
n.3: Highlighting potential tax changes is correct practice.
n.2: Plain language enhances clarity and is encouraged.

q: When disclosing costs and charges, what format must firms use?
o: Charges disclosure is optional in Non-MiFID business
Both aggregated and itemised, presented clearly
w: Firms must disclose costs in both aggregate and itemised form so clients have a full and transparent understanding of the product’s costs.

n.4: Aggregates alone lack necessary detail.
n.2: Initial costs are not sufficient disclosure.
n.1: All costs, not just variable, must be disclosed.
n.0: Non-MiFID promotions are also subject to clear disclosure requirements.

q: Under COBS, what must firms ensure about the timing of client communications?
o: That the FCA decides the communication timing for each product
That information is provided in good time before the client is bound by a contract
That communications are provided only if requested by the client
That communication timing is irrelevant provided information is accurate
That information is sent only after the client signs an agreement
w: Firms must provide information in good time before the client is bound by an agreement, giving them adequate opportunity to consider the details.

n.4: Information must be given before, not after, signing.
n.3: Timing is crucial as well as accuracy.
n.2: The duty exists regardless of client request.
n.0: The FCA does not set timing for individual products; firms are responsible.

q: Which of the following is prohibited when producing communications for retail clients?
o: Disclosing that tax rules may change
Using exaggerated terms such as 'guaranteed riches'
w: Exaggerated, misleading claims such as ‘guaranteed riches’ breach the fair, clear and not misleading requirement of COBS rules.

n.3: Balanced risk disclosures are required, not prohibited.
n.0: Benchmark comparisons are allowed if fairly presented.
n.1: Forecast warnings are required to prevent misleading impressions.
n.2: Tax change warnings are compliant, not prohibited.

q: What must be included when presenting performance information to retail clients?
o: A guarantee that future returns will match past results
A clear statement that past performance is not a reliable guide to the future
Performance data limited to one quarter
Only the top-performing years of data
w: Any inclusion of past performance must carry the clear warning that it is not a reliable indicator of future results, ensuring clients are not misled.

n.0: Future returns cannot be guaranteed.
n.4: Cherry-picking years would mislead.
n.2: Figures must reflect charges to be realistic.
n.3: Performance must cover an appropriate multi-year period.

q: Which rule applies equally to MiFID and Non-MiFID business when communicating with clients?
o: All communications must be fair, clear and not misleading
Promotions can rely solely on disclaimers
Only benefits of products need to be disclosed
w: The central principle of fairness, clarity and non-misleading communication applies to all FCA-regulated business, whether MiFID or Non-MiFID.

n.3: Risks as well as benefits must be disclosed.
n.0: Guarantees are prohibited unless genuinely risk-free.
n.4: Understanding is essential, not optional.
n.2: Disclaimers cannot replace balanced content.

q: Which of the following BEST describes the FCA’s aim with communication rules under COBS?
o: To harmonise with advertising industry practices
To ensure clients receive balanced, comprehensible and accurate information
To allow firms flexibility to omit risks
To restrict communications to professional clients only
w: The FCA’s objective is to protect consumers by ensuring communications give a balanced, clear and accurate picture of financial products and services.

n.0: Profitability is not the FCA’s aim; client protection is.
n.3: Omitting risks would breach FCA standards.
n.1: The rules extend beyond advertising practices to regulatory standards.
n.4: Rules apply to all client types, not just professionals.

q: What is the primary purpose of the FCA financial promotion rules under COBS 4.1?
o: To align with advertising industry standards only
To ensure clients receive fair, clear and not misleading information
To remove the need for disclosure of risks
w: The financial promotion rules exist to ensure all communications are fair, clear and not misleading so that clients can make informed decisions about financial products and services.

n.3: Rules cannot guarantee performance outcomes; they regulate disclosure standards.
n.0: The aim is client protection, not firm profitability.
n.4: Disclosure of risks is essential and cannot be removed.
n.1: They are regulatory standards, not limited to advertising codes.

q: Which FCA Principle for Businesses is directly reinforced by the financial promotion rules?
w: The rules support Principle 6, which requires firms to treat customers fairly, by ensuring they receive balanced and understandable information about products and services.

n.2: Integrity underpins all principles but the promotion rules specifically support fairness to customers.
n.3: Management and control relate to internal governance, not promotions.
n.0: Conflicts of interest are managed under other COBS sections.
n.1: Client asset protection is addressed elsewhere, not through promotions.

q: How does Principle 7 ('Communications with clients') relate to financial promotion rules?
o: It applies only to professional clients
It requires that all communications are fair, clear and not misleading
It allows firms to prioritise benefits over risks
It applies only to investment products, not services
It exempts digital promotions from regulation
w: Principle 7 underlines that all client communications must be fair, clear and not misleading, which forms the foundation of the COBS 4.1 financial promotion rules.

n.2: Communications must give balanced treatment to risks and benefits.
n.0: Principle 7 applies to all client types, not just professionals.
n.4: Digital promotions are equally covered under the rules.
n.3: The principle applies across products and services alike.

q: Which of the following BEST describes the application of the financial promotion rules under COBS 4.1?
o: They apply only to advice, not promotions
They apply only when requested by the client
They apply only when the FCA pre-approves material
They apply to all forms of client communication, regardless of medium
They apply only to printed material
w: COBS 4.1 applies to all communications with clients, including digital, verbal and printed, ensuring consistent consumer protection across mediums.

n.4: Promotions in all formats, not just print, are covered.
n.0: Rules extend beyond advice to all promotional material.
n.2: Most promotions do not require FCA pre-approval; compliance is the firm’s duty.
n.1: Communications must comply at all times, not just when requested.

q: What do the financial promotion rules primarily seek to prevent?
o: The disclosure of charges and fees
The use of plain language in advertising
Clients being misled into unsuitable investments
w: The rules aim to stop clients being misled into inappropriate or unsuitable investments through unclear, biased or incomplete communications.

n.1: Profit-making is not the focus; preventing client detriment is.
n.3: Plain language is encouraged, not prevented.
n.0: Benchmark comparisons are allowed if fair and balanced.
n.2: Fees and charges must be disclosed; their concealment is not the purpose.

q: Why is the relationship between financial promotion rules and Principle 6 important?
o: It removes the need for disclosure of charges
It allows firms to omit risk information if positive
It limits the rules to professional clients only
It ensures clients are treated fairly through transparent communication
It guarantees firms will achieve higher sales
w: Principle 6 requires firms to treat customers fairly, and financial promotion rules ensure this by mandating balanced, transparent and fair information in communications.

n.4: Higher sales are not the FCA’s objective; fairness to clients is.
n.0: Charges must be disclosed in full; they cannot be hidden.
n.2: The rules apply to retail and professional clients, not just professionals.
n.1: Omitting risk information would directly breach the fairness requirement.

q: Which of the following would be considered a breach of Principle 7 in financial promotions?
o: Disclosing charges in itemised and aggregate form
Presenting both risks and rewards with equal prominence
Translating material into plain language for retail clients
Using technical jargon that confuses the intended audience
Providing clear warnings about tax treatment
w: Principle 7 requires communications to be clear and comprehensible; using jargon that confuses clients breaches this obligation.

n.4: Tax disclosures are appropriate and required.
n.0: Charges disclosure is compliant, not a breach.
n.1: Balanced risk-reward presentation is required under Principle 7.
n.2: Plain language supports clarity and compliance.

q: How do the financial promotion rules interact with the FCA’s consumer protection objective?
o: They restrict access to financial services for retail clients
They ensure clients receive the information needed to make informed choices
They guarantee profits for regulated firms
They remove the requirement for firms to explain product risks
They make promotions exempt from FCA oversight
w: The financial promotion rules protect consumers by ensuring communications are fair, clear and not misleading, helping clients make properly informed decisions.

n.2: Firm profitability is not the aim; client protection is.
n.3: Risks must always be disclosed clearly, not omitted.
n.0: The rules do not restrict access but improve client understanding.
n.4: All promotions remain subject to FCA regulation.

q: Which of the following BEST illustrates compliance with Principle 6 in a financial promotion?
o: Highlighting benefits only to attract attention
Providing only gross figures without charges
Disclosing all costs and charges in a transparent manner
Relying on small print to disclose risks
w: Principle 6 requires treating customers fairly, which is demonstrated by transparent disclosure of all costs and charges so clients fully understand the impact on returns.

n.1: Highlighting benefits alone would mislead clients.
n.4: Small print for risks does not satisfy fairness or clarity.
n.0: Exaggerated claims would breach both Principle 6 and 7.
n.2: Gross figures alone without charges do not provide fairness.

q: Which of the following is an application of Principle 7 to digital promotions?
o: Exempting digital media from COBS 4.1 rules
Permitting omission of risks in banner adverts
Ensuring online adverts are fair, clear and not misleading
Allowing firms to exaggerate benefits on social media
Limiting Principle 7 to printed communications only
w: Principle 7 applies equally to digital media; firms must ensure that online adverts, banners and social media promotions are fair, clear and not misleading.

n.3: Exaggerating benefits breaches clarity and fairness obligations.
n.1: Risks must be disclosed clearly, even in short formats.
n.4: Principle 7 covers all mediums, not just print.
n.0: Digital communications are fully subject to COBS rules.

q: Which of the following statements about the scope of financial promotion rules under COBS 4.1 is correct?
o: They apply only when advice is provided
They apply only to prospectuses and formal documents
They apply only to high-value products
They apply to all communications with clients, whether solicited or unsolicited
They apply only if the FCA gives pre-approval
w: The rules under COBS 4.1 apply to all forms of communication with clients, regardless of medium or whether the client solicited the information.

n.1: They extend beyond prospectuses to all communications.
n.2: They apply regardless of product value.
n.0: They apply to both advice and promotions.
n.4: Most promotions do not require FCA pre-approval; firms are responsible for compliance.

q: How do the financial promotion rules support the FCA’s objective of market integrity?
o: By encouraging firms to compete primarily on advertising spend
By preventing misleading promotions that distort market behaviour
By ensuring firms maximise their profits
By exempting professional clients from regulation
By requiring firms to offer only low-risk products
w: By ensuring promotions are accurate and fair, the rules prevent misleading claims that could undermine confidence and distort investor behaviour in the market.

n.2: Profit maximisation is not the regulatory objective.
n.4: Firms may still offer higher-risk products if appropriately disclosed.
n.0: The rules aim at integrity and fairness, not advertising competition.
n.3: Professional clients are also within scope of Principles 6 and 7.

q: Which would demonstrate a breach of the financial promotion rules under COBS 4.1?
o: Disclosing charges in both itemised and aggregated form
Providing a balanced comparison with benchmarks
Presenting risks and benefits side by side
Highlighting benefits prominently while disclosing risks only in small print
Making clear that tax treatment depends on personal circumstances
w: Hiding risks in small print while highlighting benefits breaches the fair, clear and not misleading requirement central to COBS 4.1.

n.2: Balanced treatment of risks and benefits is compliant.
n.1: Fair benchmark comparisons are allowed.
n.0: Clear cost disclosure is required, not a breach.
n.4: Tax treatment disclosures are necessary, not prohibited.

q: What is the link between financial promotion rules and Principle 6?
o: They apply only to non-retail clients
They help ensure customers are treated fairly by preventing misleading communications
They exempt firms from disclosing charges
They allow firms to use disclaimers as the main disclosure method
w: Financial promotion rules uphold Principle 6 by ensuring clients are not misled and are treated fairly through transparent and balanced communications.

n.4: The rules aim to protect clients, not guarantee firm returns.
n.2: Charges must always be disclosed in communications.
n.0: They apply across retail and non-retail clients.
n.3: Disclaimers cannot replace balanced, fair content.

q: What is the consequence for a firm if its financial promotions breach Principle 7?
o: The rules do not apply to online communications
The promotion will automatically be disregarded by clients
The promotion becomes valid if a disclaimer is added later
The firm may face FCA enforcement action and reputational damage
w: Breaches of Principle 7 can result in FCA enforcement action, fines, and loss of trust, as communications that mislead undermine market integrity and consumer protection.

n.1: Clients may be influenced by misleading promotions; they do not automatically disregard them.
n.2: The FCA does not guarantee compensation in such cases.
n.3: Adding disclaimers after distribution does not remedy breaches.
n.0: Online communications are fully subject to the rules.

q: How do financial promotion rules align with the FCA’s Treating Customers Fairly (TCF) initiative?
o: They require firms to provide clear, balanced information so customers can make informed decisions
They remove the obligation to disclose costs
They apply only where a firm is providing advice
They allow reliance solely on generic disclaimers
They allow firms to highlight only positive aspects of products
w: The rules align with TCF by ensuring clients receive the balanced, accurate information they need to make fair choices about financial products.

n.4: Firms cannot highlight positives without risks; this would mislead.
n.1: Costs must always be disclosed clearly.
n.2: The rules apply regardless of whether advice is given.
n.3: Generic disclaimers alone are not sufficient.

q: Which of the following is TRUE about financial promotions and COBS 4.1?
o: They only apply to products over a certain value
They must always be fair, clear and not misleading
They can omit risk disclosures if the product is low risk
They are exempt from regulation if sent by email
They can guarantee investment outcomes if FCA authorised
w: The fundamental rule of COBS 4.1 is that all promotions must be fair, clear and not misleading, regardless of medium or product type.

n.3: Email communications are subject to the same rules as all other media.
n.4: FCA authorisation does not permit guarantees of outcomes.
n.2: Even low-risk products must have risk disclosures.
n.0: The rules apply to all products, not just high-value ones.

q: Why is small-print disclosure of risks insufficient under COBS 4.1?
o: Because Principle 6 eliminates the need for disclosure
Because clients are assumed not to read risk information
Because the FCA requires risk disclosures only for derivatives
Because disclaimers automatically override FCA rules
Because risks must be given equal prominence to benefits
w: COBS requires risks to be presented with equal prominence to benefits so that clients are not misled by an unbalanced impression of the product.

n.3: Disclaimers do not override FCA requirements.
n.1: Firms cannot assume clients ignore risk disclosures; they must be made prominent.
n.2: The requirement applies to all products, not only derivatives.
n.0: Principle 6 reinforces the need for disclosure; it does not remove it.

q: Which of the following best shows compliance with both Principle 6 and 7?
o: Promoting only gross returns without charges
Guaranteeing that a product will double in value
Using disclaimers instead of balanced information
Providing balanced, clear, and transparent financial promotions
w: Compliance with Principles 6 and 7 requires communications that are balanced, transparent and easily understood, ensuring clients are treated fairly and not misled.

n.1: Guaranteeing returns misleads clients and breaches rules.
n.0: Gross returns alone are not sufficient disclosure.
n.3: Best-case scenarios without balance mislead clients.
n.2: Disclaimers cannot replace balanced, clear content.

q: What is the overarching regulatory objective behind linking COBS 4.1 with Principles 6 and 7?
o: To guarantee high returns for investors
To allow firms flexibility to market however they choose
To simplify FCA supervision by reducing disclosure
To protect consumers through fair treatment and clear communication
w: The combined effect of COBS 4.1 and Principles 6 and 7 is to protect consumers by ensuring they are treated fairly and provided with clear, non-misleading information.

n.4: The aim is not to limit competition, but to improve client protection.
n.0: High returns cannot be guaranteed by regulation.
n.2: Disclosure requirements are increased, not reduced.
n.1: Firms must comply with strict rules, not market freely.

q: According to COBS 4.3, what is the key requirement for all financial promotions?
o: They must guarantee the accuracy of investment returns
They must be approved by the FCA in every case
They must be clearly identifiable as a financial promotion
They must only be directed to professional clients
They must exclude risk warnings if the product is simple
w: COBS 4.3 requires that all financial promotions are clearly identifiable as such, ensuring clients understand they are being presented with a promotional communication.

n.0: Promotions cannot guarantee returns; they must be balanced and accurate.
n.1: Not every promotion requires FCA pre-approval; firms are responsible for compliance.
n.3: The rule applies to retail and professional clients alike.
n.4: Risk warnings must never be excluded, regardless of product simplicity.

q: Why does COBS 4.3 require promotions to be clearly identified?
o: To avoid the need for risk disclosures
To prevent clients mistaking promotions for impartial information
To exempt online adverts from regulation
To allow firms to use disclaimers instead of balance
To ensure firms maximise product sales
w: The rule exists to ensure clients recognise promotional content and do not confuse it with impartial advice or factual material.

n.4: The aim is consumer protection, not maximising sales.
n.0: Risk disclosures remain mandatory.
n.3: Disclaimers alone cannot replace balance and fairness.
n.2: The requirement applies equally to online promotions.

q: Which of the following would breach COBS 4.3?
o: Presenting marketing material as impartial research
Disclosing costs in both aggregated and itemised form
Using plain language to explain features
Labelling content clearly as a promotion
w: COBS 4.3 prohibits disguising promotions as neutral content such as research, as this misleads clients about the nature of the communication.

n.4: Clear labelling is compliant and required.
n.1: Balanced presentation is part of compliance.
n.3: Plain language supports clarity.
n.2: Full cost disclosure aligns with FCA requirements.

q: Under COBS 4.3, how should firms present a promotion that appears within factual content?
o: It may omit identification if the audience is professional
It must be clearly distinguished from factual or impartial information
It can rely on disclaimers hidden in footnotes
It must replace factual content entirely
It can be blended seamlessly to appear more persuasive
w: Promotional content must be separated and clearly identified so that clients can distinguish it from factual or impartial information.

n.4: Blending with factual content misleads clients and breaches rules.
n.0: The requirement applies to all clients, not just retail.
n.3: Factual content can remain; promotions must just be clearly marked.
n.2: Footnote disclaimers are insufficient to identify promotional content.

q: What is the relationship between COBS 4.3 and Principle 7?
o: Principle 7 requires that clients are not misled about whether content is promotional
Principle 7 allows firms to hide promotional content within factual reports
Principle 7 eliminates the need for risk disclosures
Principle 7 exempts firms from identifying promotions
Principle 7 applies only to institutional clients
w: Principle 7 requires communications to be fair, clear and not misleading, which includes ensuring that clients understand when material is promotional.

n.3: Principle 7 reinforces, rather than removes, the need to identify promotions.
n.1: Hiding promotional content breaches the principle.
n.4: Principle 7 applies across client types, not only institutions.
n.2: Risk disclosures are still required alongside promotions.

q: Which of the following is an example of a compliant action under COBS 4.3?
o: Implying that a promotion is FCA-endorsed
Sending out performance data without context or labelling
Mixing research and promotion without distinction
Using small print disclaimers to identify promotional material
Labelling a marketing email subject line with ‘advertisement’
w: Clearly labelling marketing content, such as with ‘advertisement’, complies with the rule that promotions must be clearly identifiable as such.

n.1: Performance data must be labelled if used for promotional purposes.
n.2: Mixing research with promotions without clarity misleads clients.
n.3: Small print disclaimers are insufficient for compliance.
n.0: Promotions cannot suggest FCA endorsement.

q: Why does the FCA place emphasis on identifying promotions clearly?
o: To allow firms flexibility to design attractive adverts
To ensure clients understand when content may be persuasive rather than impartial
To limit disclosures to professional clients only
To exempt digital platforms from oversight
w: Clients must be able to tell when information is promotional so they can interpret it as persuasive material rather than impartial guidance.

n.1: The focus is consumer protection, not flexibility for firms.
n.0: The rules increase, not reduce, FCA oversight.
n.3: The rules apply to all clients, not just professionals.
n.4: Digital promotions are equally covered under FCA rules.

q: What would be an FCA concern if promotions are not identified as such?
o: Institutional clients may be exempt from COBS
Firms may lose market share to competitors
Clients may confuse marketing with independent advice
The FCA would not be able to levy supervisory fees
w: Failure to identify promotions risks misleading clients into thinking the information is impartial or advisory when it is promotional in nature.

n.2: Market share is not the regulatory concern; consumer protection is.
n.0: Advertising costs are irrelevant to the regulatory standard.
n.1: COBS applies broadly, not just to retail clients.
n.4: FCA supervisory fees are unrelated to promotion identification.

q: What is the potential regulatory outcome if a firm disguises promotions as impartial research?
o: The firm is allowed to continue until audited
FCA enforcement action for breaching COBS 4.3
The client bears responsibility for misinterpretation
w: Disguising promotions as research misleads clients and breaches COBS 4.3, exposing the firm to FCA enforcement action and potential penalties.

n.4: There is no automatic approval; the firm would be in breach.
n.2: Principle 6 strengthens disclosure, not exemption.
n.3: The firm, not the client, is responsible for compliance.
n.0: Firms cannot continue breaching until audited; breaches attract immediate regulatory risk.

q: Which of the following BEST describes compliance with COBS 4.3?
o: Making sure clients can clearly recognise promotional content
Providing disclaimers only in small print
Ensuring promotions are persuasive enough to increase sales
w: Compliance means clients must be able to easily identify when content is promotional so they can treat it appropriately as marketing material.

n.4: The focus is clarity, not persuasiveness.
n.2: Outcomes cannot be guaranteed under FCA rules.
n.0: Online promotions are fully covered by regulation.
n.3: Small print disclaimers do not meet identification requirements.

q: Which of the following is a key exception to the financial promotion rules under COBS 4.8?
o: All communications made to retail clients
Communications to certified high net worth individuals
Communications made outside the UK to UK clients
w: One key exception under COBS and the Financial Promotion Order (FPO) is communications directed to certified high net worth individuals, provided strict criteria are met.

n.2: Social media communications are regulated; they are not exempt.
n.4: Labelling a message as 'educational' does not create an exemption.
n.3: Cross-border communications to UK clients remain within scope.
n.0: Retail client communications are subject to stricter rules, not exemptions.

q: Which statute sets out key exemptions to financial promotion rules that supplement COBS?
o: The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order
w: The Financial Promotion Order (FPO) made under FSMA 2000 sets out specific exemptions to the financial promotion rules that operate alongside COBS provisions.

n.3: The Companies Act covers corporate governance, not financial promotions.
n.1: The DPA relates to personal data processing, not promotions.
n.4: The CJA deals with insider dealing, not promotions.
n.2: The Bribery Act regulates corruption, not financial promotion rules.

q: Which client type may financial promotions be sent to without breaching rules, under certain FPO exemptions?
o: Clients outside the UK by default
Any member of the general public
w: FPO exemptions allow promotions to be directed to certified sophisticated investors who meet strict qualifying criteria, without breaching the general restriction.

n.4: The general public are protected and remain fully covered by the restriction.
n.0: Retail clients cannot be promoted to without compliance or exemption.
n.2: Minors are not a recognised exempt category.
n.3: Cross-border communication is still subject to UK regulation.

q: Under COBS 4.1, what is the general restriction on financial promotions?
o: They are unregulated when directed online
They may be sent to retail clients without conditions
They can only be made orally to avoid regulation
They may be freely communicated if labelled clearly
They must not be communicated unless issued or approved by an authorised firm
w: The general rule is that financial promotions must not be made unless by an authorised person or approved by an authorised firm, to protect consumers from unauthorised activity.

n.3: Labelling alone does not exempt a communication.
n.0: Online promotions are regulated like all others.
n.2: Oral promotions are also within scope.
n.1: Retail clients require the highest protection, not exemptions.

q: Which limitation applies specifically to MiFID business under COBS?
o: MiFID communications can ignore the fair, clear and not misleading standard
MiFID communications are exempt from all promotion rules
MiFID communications are exempt if delivered via social media
MiFID communications may be targeted at any retail client without restrictions
MiFID communications must comply with stricter disclosure and balance requirements
w: COBS applies stricter obligations to MiFID business, requiring enhanced disclosures and balanced presentation of risks and benefits in all communications.

n.1: MiFID promotions are not exempt; they are more tightly regulated.
n.0: The fair, clear and not misleading standard always applies.
n.3: Retail clients remain subject to the highest protections.
n.2: Social media promotions are regulated the same way as others.

q: Which of the following groups can receive financial promotions under FPO exemptions without breaching COBS?
w: The FPO allows authorised firms to send promotions to investment professionals, provided the communication is relevant and proportionate to their expertise.

n.4: Retail clients are not exempt and require full regulatory protection.
n.3: Age alone does not provide an exemption.
n.0: Communications to UK clients are always regulated, regardless of firm location.
n.1: Unregulated introducers cannot lawfully receive exempt promotions.

q: How does the Financial Promotion Order (FPO) interact with COBS?
o: It replaces all COBS rules entirely
It allows any unauthorised person to issue promotions
It applies only to advertising on social media
It exempts firms from Principle 7 requirements
It provides statutory exemptions from the general restriction in FSMA 2000
w: The FPO works alongside COBS by setting out statutory exemptions to FSMA’s general restriction on financial promotions, such as communications to certified investors or professionals.

n.0: The FPO supplements COBS; it does not replace it.
n.2: It applies to all media, not just social media.
n.3: Principle 7 continues to apply regardless of exemption.
n.1: Only authorised persons may communicate promotions unless an exemption applies.

q: Which of the following is NOT an exemption under the FPO?
o: Communications to members of the general public without restriction
Communications to certified high net worth individuals
w: Members of the general public are not exempt; communications to them must comply fully with financial promotion rules or rely on another specific exemption.

n.0: Certified sophisticated investors are recognised under the FPO.
n.3: Investment professionals are an exempt category.
n.4: High net worth individuals can qualify under certain exemptions.
n.1: Authorised persons may issue promotions without relying on exemptions.

q: What is a limitation of MiFID financial promotion rules compared to Non-MiFID?
o: MiFID rules remove the need for fair presentation
MiFID exempts retail clients from disclosure rules
MiFID rules apply only to investment firms based outside the UK
MiFID rules only apply to printed adverts
MiFID requires stricter standards for retail client communications
w: MiFID imposes stricter obligations on firms when communicating with retail clients, including detailed disclosure of risks, costs and balanced presentation of benefits.

n.1: Retail clients remain subject to the most protective rules under MiFID.
n.3: MiFID rules cover all formats, not just print.
n.0: The fair, clear and not misleading principle remains central.
n.2: MiFID rules apply to EU/UK investment business, not only foreign firms.

q: Why is the existence of the FPO significant for authorised firms?
o: It removes the need for disclosures in retail promotions
It clarifies when communications are exempt from the financial promotion restriction
It allows firms to bypass COBS obligations entirely
It exempts social media advertising automatically
It guarantees FCA approval for promotional materials
w: The FPO provides clarity on when communications fall outside the general restriction, such as promotions to certain categories of investors, without removing the overall duty to comply with COBS.

n.2: COBS obligations still apply where relevant; the FPO does not override them.
n.4: The FPO does not provide FCA approval; firms remain responsible for compliance.
n.0: Disclosures remain necessary in retail promotions.
n.3: Social media advertising is subject to the same requirements as other media.

q: Which of the following categories is explicitly recognised as an exempt recipient under the FPO?
w: The FPO provides an exemption for communications directed at certified high net worth individuals who meet specific criteria, without breaching the restriction.

n.4: Retail clients are not exempt by default and require full compliance.
n.1: Age alone does not provide an exemption.
n.2: General public seminars are not automatically exempt.
n.3: Non-UK citizens are not exempt purely on nationality.

q: How do COBS 4.8 exemptions operate in practice?
o: They exempt all online advertisements automatically
They allow certain communications without breaching the general restriction
They apply only when the FCA confirms in writing
They allow firms to ignore MiFID requirements
They remove the need for all promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading
w: COBS 4.8 exemptions clarify situations where promotions may be made without breaching FSMA’s general restriction, while still requiring compliance with fairness standards.

n.4: The fair, clear and not misleading rule always applies.
n.0: Online advertisements remain subject to full regulation.
n.2: Written FCA approval is not a requirement for exemptions.
n.3: MiFID rules continue to apply where relevant.

q: Which of the following is an example of a communication exempted under the FPO?
o: A cold call to any consumer
An email sent to all UK households
A general marketing campaign to the public
A promotion directed to certified sophisticated investors
A social media post aimed at retail clients
w: The FPO recognises an exemption for promotions directed at certified sophisticated investors, provided the necessary statements and certifications are in place.

n.2: General public marketing requires compliance or authorisation.
n.4: Social media promotions are subject to the rules.
n.0: Cold calls to consumers are tightly restricted and not exempt.
n.1: Mass unsolicited emails do not fall under exemptions.

q: Which of the following BEST explains the limitation of exemptions for MiFID business?
o: Exemptions eliminate the need to comply with MiFID entirely
Exemptions mean risk disclosures are optional
Exemptions allow omission of costs and charges
Exemptions apply only to institutional clients under MiFID
Exemptions cannot override MiFID’s stricter disclosure requirements
w: MiFID imposes mandatory obligations on firms; exemptions under the FPO cannot remove or dilute these stricter disclosure and conduct requirements.

n.0: Exemptions do not eliminate MiFID compliance obligations.
n.3: Exemptions may apply beyond institutions; the limitation is stricter standards.
n.2: Charges must always be disclosed under MiFID.
n.1: Risk disclosures remain mandatory under MiFID.

q: Which of the following would NOT fall within an FPO exemption?
o: A communication to certified sophisticated investors
A promotion targeted to investment professionals
A communication directed at a certified high net worth individual
A communication made by an authorised person
A promotion disguised as impartial research
w: Disguising a promotion as impartial research breaches COBS 4.3 and cannot be justified under FPO exemptions.

n.2: High net worth individuals are an exempt category.
n.1: Investment professionals are covered by exemptions.
n.0: Certified sophisticated investors are recognised as exempt recipients.
n.3: Authorised persons may communicate promotions without relying on exemptions.

q: Which of the following is an example of the 'general restriction' in financial promotion rules?
o: Only retail clients are covered by the restriction
Firms may communicate freely as long as they label content clearly
Oral communications are excluded from the restriction
Overseas promotions into the UK are exempt from restriction
An unauthorised person must not communicate a promotion unless an exemption applies
w: The general restriction under FSMA 2000 states that unauthorised persons cannot make financial promotions unless an exemption under the FPO applies.

n.1: Labelling alone does not create compliance.
n.0: The restriction applies to all client categories, not just retail.
n.2: Oral communications are also within scope.
n.3: Overseas promotions to UK clients are regulated.

q: Why is the FPO particularly important for unauthorised persons?
o: It allows them to market freely without conditions
It guarantees FCA approval of their communications
It permits them to carry out regulated activities
It exempts them from all FCA rules
It provides statutory exemptions that allow them to make certain communications lawfully
w: The FPO is essential for unauthorised persons as it provides narrowly defined exemptions to the general restriction, enabling certain lawful communications.

n.2: Exemptions do not authorise firms to carry out regulated activities.
n.3: Unauthorised persons remain subject to FCA rules where applicable.
n.1: The FPO does not provide FCA approval.
n.0: Marketing is not free; strict conditions apply.

q: Which of the following categories is NOT typically covered by FPO exemptions?
w: The general public is not an exempt category; promotions to them must be approved or issued by authorised persons and comply fully with FCA standards.

n.1: Sophisticated investors are recognised under exemptions.
n.4: Internal communications to employees can be exempt.
n.0: High net worth individuals can qualify under exemptions.
n.3: Investment professionals are exempt recipients.

q: Which of the following is TRUE about the interaction between COBS and the FPO?
o: Exemptions under the FPO remove the need for risk disclosures
Exemptions under the FPO eliminate all MiFID requirements
Exemptions apply only to printed material
Exemptions permit guaranteed claims of future performance
Exemptions under the FPO do not remove the requirement that communications must be fair, clear and not misleading
w: Even when an exemption applies under the FPO, the overarching requirement remains that all communications must be fair, clear and not misleading.

n.0: Risk disclosures remain mandatory under COBS.
n.1: MiFID obligations cannot be waived by FPO exemptions.
n.2: Exemptions apply across media, not just print.
n.3: Future performance cannot be guaranteed.

q: Which of the following BEST describes the role of exemptions in the financial promotion regime?
o: They permit unlimited marketing to all clients
They are designed to encourage aggressive advertising strategies
They eliminate FCA oversight of promotions
They carve out narrow circumstances where promotions can be made without breaching FSMA restrictions
They allow firms to ignore COBS standards in retail promotions
w: Exemptions allow certain promotions to be made lawfully in narrowly defined cases, but do not remove the requirement for fairness or wider FCA oversight.

n.0: Unlimited marketing to all clients is not permitted.
n.2: The FCA continues to oversee compliance with the regime.
n.1: The purpose is protection, not aggressive advertising.

q: What overarching standard applies to all client communications under COBS 4?

w: COBS 4 requires all communications to be fair, clear and not misleading.

n.4: Maximising revenue prioritises the firm, whereas the rule centres on fairness to clients.
n.3: Full terms are not always required, while the fairness standard always applies.
n.2: Template use is not mandated, whereas fairness, clarity, and accuracy are mandatory.
n.0: Past performance is conditional and constrained, but the fairness standard applies universally.

q: Which method counts as a 'durable medium' for COBS disclosures?
w: Email that can be stored unchanged by the client qualifies as a durable medium.

n.3: A public homepage can change without notice, whereas durable media must be stable.
n.4: A newspaper cannot ensure client-controlled retention, unlike durable electronic messages.
n.0: Recordings are firm-held, not client-retainable, unlike client-retained emails.
n.2: Oral briefings are ephemeral, not durable, whereas stored emails are.

q: When making a non-written financial promotion, what must the communicator do?

n.3: All risk factors need not be read verbatim, while identification is required.
n.2: A written follow-up is not always required, but identification during the call is.
n.0: FSCS wording is context-dependent, unlike the universal identification requirement.

q: Which statement about image advertising under COBS 4 is correct?
o: It is entirely outside financial promotion rules
It must include full cost disclosures
It has limited exemptions from detailed rules
It is allowed only on print media

n.3: FCA pre-approval is not required; firms are responsible for compliance.

q: How must past performance be presented in a financial promotion?

n.2: Gross-only can mislead, whereas prominence and balance are required.
n.0: Ten years is not mandated, while warning prominence is required.
n.4: Benchmarks can be used if fair, unlike the mandatory warning requirement.
n.1: Projections are not past performance; warnings are required for past data.

q: Which audience remains subject to COBS financial promotion standards?
w: Promotions to professional clients must still be fair, clear and not misleading.

n.3: Eligible counterparty category does not exclude COBS 4 duties entirely, while fairness applies to professionals.
n.4: Jurisdiction does not remove COBS standards, whereas professional clients remain covered.
n.1: Sophistication status does not nullify rules, while professional promotions still require fairness.
n.0: Wealth alone does not disapply standards, unlike the universal fairness requirement.

q: Which statement best defines a direct offer financial promotion?
o: It must include a KID always
It is limited to postal mailings
It enables an immediate investment decision
w: A direct offer financial promotion invites and enables an immediate transactional decision by the client.

n.1: Channel is not restricted to post, whereas the decision-enabling nature defines it.
n.3: Online ads are not exempt, since enabling immediate decisions still triggers the classification.
n.0: A KID depends on product type, while the decisive feature is decision enablement.
n.2: It can apply beyond execution-only, as the key is enabling commitment.

q: Why must risk warnings be prominent in retail promotions?
o: To balance benefits with material risks
w: Prominent risk warnings ensure promotions are balanced and not misleading by offsetting highlighted benefits.

n.4: Templates are not the goal, whereas balancing risks and benefits is required.
n.0: Warnings do not replace suitability, while they support fair communications.
n.3: Costs cannot be omitted merely due to warnings; balance is the aim.
n.2: Warning prominence is about fairness, not complaint timing.

q: Who is responsible for an appointed representative’s compliant promotion?
w: The principal firm is responsible for ensuring its appointed representative’s promotions comply with COBS.

n.3: A contractor is not the regulated principal, whereas the principal bears responsibility.
n.1: Media hosts are not responsible for regulatory compliance; the principal is.
n.4: An individual salesperson acts for the AR, while the principal oversees compliance.
n.2: Manufacturers are distinct; the principal is accountable for the AR’s promotions.

q: Which comparison practice aligns with COBS 4?
w: Comparisons must be fair, using relevant and consistently applied benchmarks to avoid misleading clients.

n.1: Cherry-picking best periods misleads, whereas fairness demands balanced comparisons.
n.3: Omitting charges inflates returns, while fairness requires balanced presentation.
n.2: Changing benchmarks confuses clients, unlike consistent, relevant benchmarks.
n.0: Unrelated assets distort comparisons, while relevance and consistency are required.

q: What must a prospectus advertisement clearly state under PR 3.3?
w: PR 3.3 requires advertisements to indicate where the approved prospectus can be obtained by investors.

n.3: Personal tax illustrations are not mandatory, whereas access to the prospectus is.
n.1: Guarantees are improper; the rule focuses on prospectus availability.
n.4: Broker lists are not required, unlike the access information.
n.2: Operational cut-offs are not mandated; prospectus location is.

q: Which statement about the FCA’s approval of a prospectus must an advertisement include?
w: PR 3.3 requires stating that competent authority approval should not be understood as an endorsement of the securities.

n.3: Approval does not guarantee accuracy; it is explicitly not an endorsement.
n.1: Performance is never guaranteed; approval is not an endorsement.
n.2: Risks remain present; the required wording clarifies no endorsement.

q: How must prospectus advertisements relate to the prospectus content?
o: They must be consistent with it
They may simplify by omitting risks
They can rely on oral clarifications
w: PR 3.3 requires advertisements to be consistent with the information contained in the approved prospectus.

n.2: Omitting risks would mislead, whereas consistency requires balanced content.
n.3: Emphasising projections can mislead, while consistency with the prospectus is required.
n.1: Unapproved pricing claims risk inconsistency; alignment with the prospectus is required.
n.4: Oral clarifications cannot remedy inconsistencies; written alignment is required.

q: Who bears primary responsibility for compliance of a prospectus advertisement?
w: Responsibility rests with the issuer, offeror, or person seeking admission to trading.

n.2: Venues host admissions, whereas the issuer or offeror ensures compliance.
n.0: Media outlets disseminate content; they are not the responsible party.
n.3: Analysts produce research, while the issuer or offeror is responsible.
n.4: Investors bear no publication duty; responsibility lies with the promoter.

q: Why must prospectus advertisements present risks with equal prominence to benefits?
w: Balanced presentation avoids advertisements creating a misleading impression contrary to PR 3.3 requirements.

n.3: Underwriting costs are unrelated, whereas balance addresses misleading content.
n.0: Participation aims do not override balance; preventing mislead is required.
n.2: Timelines are regulatory, while balance targets fairness and accuracy.
n.1: Stabilization is a market practice; balance concerns advertisement integrity.

q: Which dissemination channel can be used for a PR 3.3 advertisement?
w: Advertisements may use any medium, provided PR 3.3 content and consistency requirements are met.

n.2: There is no newspaper-only rule; any compliant medium is allowed.
n.3: Websites are not exclusive channels; multiple compliant media are permitted.
n.4: TV is not the sole route; any medium may be used if compliant.

q: What must an advertisement do if it includes numerical data from the prospectus?

Use the same basis and source

n.1: Changing accounting bases distorts comparability, whereas consistency is required.

q: When referencing the prospectus in an advertisement, what aids investor access?

n.4: Physical collection creates barriers; clear access details are required.
n.3: QR codes are optional; explicit access details satisfy the requirement.
n.1: Summaries without directions hinder access, unlike clear location details.

q: Which statement best reflects the status of pre-approval advertising under PR 3.3?
o: It must omit all risk factors
It must avoid implying an approved prospectus exists

n.0: Binding offers risk misleading investors; clarity about approval is required.
n.2: Omitting risks misleads; accuracy, not omission, is required pre-approval.

q: According to COBS 4.5, what is the general rule for communications with retail clients?

They must be fair, clear and not misleading
